questions.question: **Distinguish between phase sequence and checking the direction of motor rotation. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Phase sequence concerns the maintained order of the phase conductors throughout a polyphase installation.

It can often be verified by:

- conductor identification;
- correct termination;
- systematic inspection.

Motor rotation is the **mechanical direction** in which a connected motor turns when energized.

A phase-rotation test may be required for practical commissioning of equipment, but it is not identical to verifying conductor phase sequence.

---

questions.title: Question 65 — Functional Testing
questions.question: **State six items that may require functional testing after electrical safety tests have been completed. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 66 — Expected Result vs Measured Result
questions.question: **Why should a competent tester predict an approximate result before measuring? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 67 — Very Low Live \(Z_s\)
questions.question:
A calculated circuit value from:

\[
Z_e+(R_1+R_2)
\]

is 0.92 Ω.

A live loop test gives 0.48 Ω.

Give a likely explanation. **(4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 68 — Broken Neutral: Voltage Clue
questions.answer:
A likely fault is:

\[
\boxed{\text{broken/open neutral upstream of the socket}}
\]

The line conductor remains connected to the supply.

Because the neutral is broken, it no longer has a direct zero-volt reference to the supply neutral.

With the load connected, the line voltage is transferred through the lamp/load to the disconnected neutral conductor.

Therefore the local neutral can rise towards line potential.

At the faulty socket:

\[
L\approx230V
\]

and:

\[
N\approx230V
\]

relative to Earth.

The difference between them is then:

\[
L-N\approx0V
\]

so the appliance cannot receive the required potential difference and does not operate normally.

This is also a reminder that a neutral conductor must never be assumed safe merely because it is called “neutral.”

---

questions.title: Question 69 — Borrowed Neutral
questions.question: **Explain why a borrowed or shared neutral between two separately protected circuits can create a serious isolation hazard. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 70 — Why Record Test Results?
questions.question: **Give five reasons why actual test results should be recorded accurately. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 71 — Initial Verification Certificate
questions.question: Under the BS 7671 model-document system, what type of certificate is normally associated with a new installation or substantial new installation work after successful initial verification? **(3 marks)**
questions.answer:
The UK BS 7671 model document is an:

\[
\boxed{\text{Electrical Installation Certificate (EIC)}}
\]

It normally includes or is accompanied by:

- schedules of inspections;
- schedules of test results.

### EPRA Study Note

The important EPRA principle is that installation work must be properly inspected, tested, commissioned and documented.

Do not assume the UK document title is automatically the name of the Kenyan statutory form.

---

questions.title: Question 72 — Periodic Inspection Report
questions.question: Under the BS 7671 model-document system, what document records the outcome of a periodic inspection and test of an existing installation? **(3 marks)**

questions.title: Question 73 — Full Initial-Verification Scenario
questions.answer:
### (a) Calculate \(Z_s\)

\[
Z_s=Z_e+(R_1+R_2)
\]

\[
Z_s=0.32+0.58
\]

\[
\boxed{Z_s=0.90\Omega}
\]

---

### (b) Insulation resistance

Each result is:

\[
>200M\Omega
\]

Minimum:

\[
1M\Omega
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{the results are comfortably above the minimum}}
\]

They indicate very high insulation resistance.

---

### (c) RCD trip time

Measured:

\[
42ms
\]

Maximum criterion used in the question:

\[
300ms
\]

Since:

\[
42<300
\]

the RCD:

\[
\boxed{\text{satisfies the stated operating-time criterion}}
\]

---

### (d) Further checks

Suitable answers include:

1. protective-device type and rating;
2. correct supply polarity;
3. prospective fault current/breaking capacity;
4. correct operation of switches and controls;
5. voltage-drop verification;
6. equipment identification;
7. completeness of protective earthing and bonding;
8. final visual inspection;
9. circuit labelling;
10. completion of required records/certification.

A collection of good individual test results is not enough unless the **whole protective arrangement** is satisfactory.

---

questions.title: Question 74 — Practical Assessment Scenario
questions.question:
An electrician begins a test assessment by switching an MCB OFF and immediately disconnecting the circuit conductors.

Identify the main safety failure and state the correct actions that should have preceded disconnection. **(8 marks)**

questions.title: Question 75 — Three-Phase Insulation-Resistance Scenario
questions.answer:
### (a) Test voltage

The nominal system voltage is within the “up to and including 500 V” category.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{500V\text{ DC}}
\]

---

### (b) Minimum insulation resistance

From Table 64:

\[
\boxed{1M\Omega}
\]

---

### (c) Number of unique tests

For five conductors:

\[
\boxed{10}
\]

unique pairs.

---

### (d) Test sequence

#### To Earth

1. L1-E
2. L2-E
3. L3-E
4. N-E

#### To Neutral

5. L1-N
6. L2-N
7. L3-N

#### Between Lines

8. L1-L2
9. L1-L3
10. L2-L3

Working systematically prevents combinations from being missed.

---

questions.title: Question 76 — Oral Interview: Explain Testing from Start to Finish
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“You have completed a new domestic circuit. Explain how you would inspect, test and commission it from the moment you arrive at the board until handover.”**

Give a complete answer. **(20 marks)**

title: Wiring & lighting
sourceTitle: Step 5 — Lighting Circuits, One-Way/Two-Way/Intermediate Switching, Socket Circuits, Radial and Ring Final Circuits, and Practical Fault-Finding — Strengthened Distinction Edition

questions.title: Question 1 — Purpose of a Lighting Circuit
questions.question: **What is the purpose of a lighting final circuit? (3 marks)**

questions.title: Question 2 — Function of the Line Conductor
questions.question: **What is the function of the line conductor in a lighting circuit? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
The line conductor carries current from the source towards the load.

In a normal single-phase AC circuit, it is the conductor maintained at line potential relative to neutral/Earth.

Switches intended for ordinary single-pole control should normally interrupt the:

\[
\boxed{\text{line conductor}}
\]

not the neutral.

This ensures that when the switch is OFF, the downstream switched part of the lighting circuit is not intentionally left connected to the live line supply.

---

questions.title: Question 3 — Function of Neutral
questions.question: **What is the function of the neutral conductor in a normal single-phase lighting circuit? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
The neutral conductor provides the normal return path for load current to the source.

With a lamp operating:

\[
\text{line}\rightarrow\text{lamp}\rightarrow\text{neutral}
\]

forms the normal current path.

Neutral is a live conductor under BS 7671 terminology even though it is normally close to Earth potential.

Therefore neutral must not automatically be assumed safe to touch.

---

questions.title: Question 4 — Function of the CPC
questions.question: **What is the function of the CPC in a lighting circuit? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 5 — Permanent Line vs Switched Line
questions.question: **Differentiate between a permanent line conductor and a switched line conductor. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Permanent line

A permanent line conductor remains connected to the line supply whenever the circuit is energized.

It supplies:

- switches;
- control devices;
- loop connections;
- other permanent-line points.

### Switched line

A switched line becomes energized only when the relevant switch path is closed.

It carries line potential from the switch to the load.

For a simple lighting circuit:

\[
\text{permanent line}\rightarrow\text{switch}\rightarrow\text{switched line}\rightarrow\text{lamp}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 6 — Define One-Way Switching
questions.question: **What is one-way lighting control? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
One-way switching means:

\[
\boxed{\text{one switch controls one lighting point or lighting group from one location}}
\]

The switch either:

- completes the line path to the lamp;
- or opens the line path.

Therefore:

- switch ON → circuit complete → lamp operates;
- switch OFF → line path open → lamp does not operate.

---

questions.title: Question 7 — One-Way Switch Terminals
questions.question:
A typical one-way switch uses COM and L1 terminals.

**Explain how they are used. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A typical connection is:

- permanent line into:

\[
\boxed{COM}
\]

- switched line out from:

\[
\boxed{L1}
\]

When the switch is ON:

\[
COM\leftrightarrow L1
\]

and current can flow to the lamp.

When the switch is OFF, the connection is open.

Depending on the switch design and manufacturer, terminal markings can vary, so the actual accessory markings should always be checked.

---

questions.title: Question 8 — Current Path with One-Way Switch ON
questions.question: **Describe the current path when a one-way lighting switch is ON. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 9 — Current Path with Switch OFF
questions.question: **What happens electrically when the one-way switch is OFF? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The switch opens the line path.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{the circuit to the lamp is incomplete}}
\]

No normal load current can flow through the lamp.

The neutral may still be connected to the luminaire.

The permanent-line conductor up to the switch remains energized while the circuit itself remains supplied.

This is why simply switching a light OFF is **not safe isolation**.

---

questions.title: Question 10 — Neutral Switched Instead of Line
questions.question:
A one-way switch has accidentally been connected in the neutral conductor.

The lamp still switches ON and OFF.

**Explain why the arrangement is unsafe. (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
Opening the neutral stops normal current, so the lamp appears to operate correctly.

However, the line conductor remains permanently connected to the lamp/fitting.

Therefore, when the switch is OFF:

- the lamp may appear dead;
- but parts of the fitting can remain connected to line potential.

A person changing a lamp or working on the luminaire could receive an electric shock.

The switch should interrupt the:

\[
\boxed{\text{line conductor}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 11 — One-Way Circuit Fault: Lamp Never Turns On
questions.question:
A one-way lighting circuit is supplied correctly, but the lamp never illuminates.

**State six faults that could cause this. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 12 — One-Way Circuit Fault: Lamp Permanently ON
questions.question:
A lamp remains ON regardless of the switch position.

**Give four likely causes. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 13 — Define Two-Way Switching
questions.question: **What is two-way switching? Give a practical example. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 14 — Two-Way Switch Terminals
questions.answer:
### COM

The common terminal connects internally to either L1 or L2 depending on switch position.

### L1 and L2

These are the two alternative switched paths.

In a normal two-way arrangement:

- L1 and L2 of one switch are connected to corresponding switching conductors at the other switch;
- these interconnecting conductors are commonly called **strappers**.

The common terminals are used for the incoming permanent line and outgoing switched line, depending on the wiring method.

---

questions.title: Question 15 — What Are Strappers?
questions.question: **Define strapper conductors in a two-way lighting circuit. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Strappers are the two conductors connecting the alternative switch paths between two-way switches.

They normally connect:

\[
L1\leftrightarrow L1
\]

and:

\[
L2\leftrightarrow L2
\]

or the equivalent arrangement required by the chosen wiring method.

The two-way switches select between these paths.

The lamp operates when the switch positions create a complete path from permanent line to switched line.

---

questions.title: Question 16 — How Two-Way Switching Works
questions.question: **Explain, without relying on a memorized diagram, how two switches can control one lamp. (8 marks)**
questions.answer:
Each two-way switch is a changeover switch.

Its COM terminal connects to either:

- L1;
- or L2.

The two switches are linked by two strapper conductors.

One switch receives the permanent line at its COM.

The other switch provides the switched line from its COM to the lamp.

If both switches select a path that creates electrical continuity through the strapper system:

\[
\boxed{\text{lamp ON}}
\]

If the selected paths do not create continuity:

\[
\boxed{\text{lamp OFF}}
\]

Operating either switch changes which strapper path is selected and therefore changes the lamp state.

---

questions.title: Question 17 — Two-Way Truth Table
questions.question:
Two two-way switches are labelled A and B.

Explain the general ON/OFF pattern when either switch is changed. **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The exact physical up/down position depends on how the switches are installed, but the essential principle is:

\[
\boxed{\text{operating either switch reverses the lamp state}}
\]

Therefore:

- if lamp is ON → operate either switch → OFF;
- if lamp is OFF → operate either switch → ON.

The system is based on changeover continuity, not on both switches simply being “ON switches.”

---

questions.title: Question 18 — Broken Strapper
questions.question:
One strapper conductor in a two-way lighting circuit becomes open-circuit.

**Describe the possible symptom. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
The lamp may:

- work only with particular combinations of the two switches;
- fail to operate from one position;
- appear to work from one switch but not reliably from the other.

This occurs because one of the two alternative paths has been lost.

The remaining strapper may still provide a complete circuit in certain switch positions.

Therefore an intermittent-looking two-way problem can actually be a permanent open circuit in one strapper.

---

questions.title: Question 19 — Incorrect COM Connection
questions.question:
A two-way switch has the permanent line mistakenly connected to L1 rather than COM.

**What type of symptom may occur? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The two-way system will no longer operate according to the intended changeover logic.

Possible symptoms include:

- lamp only works in certain unusual switch combinations;
- one switch appears ineffective in some positions;
- lamp may not toggle correctly from both locations.

The correct function depends on the common terminal being used as the changeover input/output.

---

questions.title: Question 20 — Testing a Two-Way Circuit
questions.question: **Why must both switch positions be operated when checking continuity or operation of a two-way lighting circuit? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 21 — Purpose of an Intermediate Switch
questions.question: **When is an intermediate switch used? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
An intermediate switch is used when a lighting point must be controlled from:

\[
\boxed{\text{three or more locations}}
\]

For control from three locations, the normal arrangement is:

\[
\boxed{\text{two-way}\rightarrow\text{intermediate}\rightarrow\text{two-way}}
\]

Additional intermediate switches can be inserted for additional control locations.

---

questions.title: Question 22 — How an Intermediate Switch Works
questions.question: **Explain the operating principle of an intermediate switch. (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
An intermediate switch has four switching terminals associated with the two strapper paths.

It changes the relationship between the incoming and outgoing strappers.

In one position it connects the paths approximately:

\[
A\rightarrow A,\qquad B\rightarrow B
\]

In the other position it crosses them:

\[
A\rightarrow B,\qquad B\rightarrow A
\]

Therefore the intermediate switch changes the continuity path without being the start or end common switch.

Operating it reverses the lamp state when used correctly between two two-way switches.

---

questions.title: Question 23 — Three-Location Lighting Arrangement
questions.question: **Describe the arrangement required to control one lamp from three locations. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

1. a two-way switch at the first control point;
2. an intermediate switch at the middle point;
3. a two-way switch at the final point.

The permanent line enters one end two-way switch.

The switched line to the lamp leaves the other end two-way switch.

The strapper pair passes through the intermediate switch.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{2-way}\rightarrow\text{intermediate}\rightarrow\text{2-way}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 24 — Four Control Locations
questions.question: **How would you modify the arrangement to control the same lamp from four locations? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

- one two-way switch at each end;
- two intermediate switches between them.

Arrangement:

\[
\boxed{\text{2-way}\rightarrow\text{intermediate}\rightarrow\text{intermediate}\rightarrow\text{2-way}}
\]

More intermediate switches may be added if still more control points are required.

---

questions.title: Question 25 — Intermediate-Switch Fault
questions.question:
An intermediate switch is incorrectly wired so that only one strapper path is passed through.

**What symptoms might appear? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 26 — Factors in Luminaire Selection
questions.question: **State eight factors that should be considered when selecting a luminaire. (8 marks)**

questions.title: Question 27 — Class I Luminaire
questions.question: **What is a Class I luminaire, and what protective provision does it require? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Related formal BS 7671 definition

The uploaded Part 2 defines **Class I equipment** as equipment in which protection against electric shock does not rely on basic insulation only, but includes means for connecting exposed-conductive-parts to a protective conductor in the fixed wiring.

A Class I luminaire therefore uses basic insulation together with protective earthing.

Accessible conductive metal parts are connected to a protective conductor.

Therefore it requires an effective:

\[
\boxed{\text{CPC/earth connection}}
\]

If a line conductor faults to the metal enclosure, the CPC provides the fault-current path required for protective disconnection.

---

questions.title: Question 28 — Class II Luminaire
questions.question: **What is a Class II luminaire? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A Class II luminaire relies on:

\[
\boxed{\text{double or reinforced insulation}}
\]

rather than protective earthing as its protective construction.

### Definition-source note

The uploaded scan clearly contains the Class II concept in the double/reinforced-insulation section, but the OCR mis-renders one heading. This strengthened file therefore does **not** present the garbled OCR heading as an exact quotation. The technical meaning is retained without falsely claiming a clean verbatim definition.

as the protective measure.

It does not rely on a protective-earth connection in the same way as Class I equipment.

However, installing Class II equipment does not automatically correct a defective fixed-wiring system.

The underlying circuit still has to be assessed and comply with the relevant requirements.

---

questions.title: Question 29 — Outdoor Luminaire
questions.question:
A luminaire is to be installed outside where it will be exposed to rain.

**Why is ordinary indoor electrical suitability not enough? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 30 — Domestic Lighting RCD Requirement
questions.question: Under the Brown Book BS 7671 framework, what additional protection is required for AC final circuits supplying luminaires in domestic premises? **(4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 31 — Why an RCD Does Not Replace the CPC
questions.question: **Explain why fitting a 30 mA RCD does not mean a Class I luminaire can be installed without a CPC. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
The protective measures perform different functions.

The CPC provides:

\[
\boxed{\text{the intended fault-current path}}
\]

The RCD detects residual current imbalance and disconnects when its operating conditions are met.

A Class I luminaire is designed to have its exposed metalwork connected to protective Earth.

Removing the CPC defeats the intended protective construction of the equipment.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{RCD protection supplements; it does not casually replace required protective earthing}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 32 — Define a Socket-Outlet
questions.question: **What is the purpose of a socket-outlet in an installation? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Formal BS 7671 definition

The uploaded Part 2 defines a **Socket-outlet** as:

> **“A device, provided with female contacts, which is intended to be installed with the fixed wiring, and intended to receive a plug.”**

In practical terms, it provides a point at which portable or movable electrical equipment can be connected to the fixed installation.

It allows equipment to be:

- connected;
- disconnected;
- moved;
- replaced

without permanently altering the fixed wiring.

---

questions.title: Question 33 — Final Circuit vs Distribution Circuit
questions.question: **Differentiate between a final circuit and a distribution circuit. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Final circuit

A final circuit directly supplies:

- current-using equipment;
- socket-outlets;
- or other final loads.

### Distribution circuit

A distribution circuit supplies another:

\[
\boxed{\text{distribution board or distribution point}}
\]

rather than directly supplying the final load.

Example:

\[
\text{main board}\rightarrow\text{sub-board}
\]

is a distribution circuit.

\[
\text{sub-board}\rightarrow\text{socket}
\]

is a final circuit.

---

questions.title: Question 34 — Radial Circuit
questions.question: **Define a radial final circuit. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A radial final circuit leaves the protective device and passes through the required outlets or points without returning to the same protective-device terminal.

Conceptually:

\[
\boxed{\text{DB}\rightarrow A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C\rightarrow\text{end}}
\]

Each part of the circuit carries the load current downstream of that point.

The cable and protective device must therefore be selected so that the circuit is adequately protected throughout its route.

---

questions.title: Question 35 — Ring Final Circuit
questions.question: **Define a ring final circuit. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Formal BS 7671 definition

The uploaded Part 2 defines a **Ring final circuit** as:

> **“A final circuit arranged in the form of a ring and connected to a single point of supply.”**

In practical terms, the circuit leaves the protective device, passes through the socket/accessory points, and returns to the same origin/protective device to form a closed ring.

Conceptually:

\[
\boxed{\text{DB}\rightarrow A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C\rightarrow\text{DB}}
\]

Each point on the ring is connected to the origin by two conductor paths.

Under normal conditions, load current is shared between the two legs of the ring according to the load position and conductor impedances.

---

questions.title: Question 36 — Radial vs Ring
questions.question: **State four differences between a radial final circuit and a ring final circuit. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
| Radial | Ring |
|---|---|
| Leaves origin and terminates at final point | Returns to origin |
| One principal supply path to each downstream point | Two paths around ring |
| Current does not intentionally divide around two ring legs | Load current divides between ring legs |
| Open conductor normally disconnects downstream section | Open ring conductor may leave outlets operating as an unintended radial arrangement |

The ring therefore requires specific continuity verification.

---

questions.title: Question 37 — Regulation 433.1.204
questions.question: Under the Brown Book framework, state the important conditions for the common BS 1363 ring-final-circuit arrangement permitted by Regulation 433.1.204. **(8 marks)**

questions.title: Question 38 — Why Can a 2.5 mm² Ring Be Protected at 32 A?
questions.question: **Explain the engineering reason why a compliant ring final circuit can use a 30/32 A protective device even though the current-carrying capacity of one 2.5 mm² leg may be less than 32 A. (7 marks)**
questions.answer:
The load is supplied through two paths around the ring.

At a socket located on the ring, current divides between the two legs according to their impedances.

Therefore one conductor is not expected to carry the entire 32 A circuit load continuously under the intended arrangement.

Regulation 433.1.204 permits this special arrangement provided:

- conductor size is not below the specified minimum;
- installed cable current capacity is adequate;
- load distribution does not cause long-duration overload of one part of the ring.

The ring configuration is therefore a **designed exception** to the simple radial rule that each cable must individually carry the full protective-device rating.

---

questions.title: Question 39 — Broken Ring Conductor
questions.question:
A ring final circuit has an open line conductor at one point.

Most socket-outlets still work.

**Explain why this fault is dangerous. (7 marks)**
questions.answer:
When the ring conductor opens, the circuit may no longer operate as a true ring.

It can become two radial sections supplied from the same protective device.

Socket-outlets may therefore continue to work, which can hide the fault.

However, one conductor leg may now be required to carry substantially more current than intended.

A 32 A protective device may remain in place while the circuit is no longer sharing current correctly.

This can result in:

- cable overload;
- overheating;
- damaged insulation;
- fire risk.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{“all sockets work” does not prove ring continuity}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 40 — Open CPC on a Ring
questions.question:
A ring final circuit has a break in one CPC leg but line and neutral remain intact.

**Why may the fault remain hidden during ordinary use? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Normal operating current flows through:

- line;
- neutral.

The CPC normally carries no load current.

Therefore all appliances may operate normally.

However, protective conductor continuity has been weakened or lost around part of the ring.

During an earth fault:

- the effective fault path may have higher impedance;
- protective disconnection may be slower;
- some accessories may lose effective earthing.

This is why the CPC ring is specifically tested for continuity.

---

questions.title: Question 41 — Load at Midpoint
questions.question:
A 20 A load is connected exactly halfway around an ideal ring whose two legs have equal resistance.

Approximately how much current flows in each leg? **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Because the two paths have equal resistance, the load current divides equally.

Therefore:

\[
I_1=I_2=\frac{20}{2}
\]

\[
\boxed{I_1=10A,\qquad I_2=10A}
\]

This is an idealized example.

Real ring circuits have multiple loads at different points, so current sharing varies with load position and conductor impedance.

---

questions.title: Question 42 — Load Near One End
questions.question:
A 20 A load is connected very close to one end of a ring.

Will the current necessarily divide 10 A/10 A? Explain. **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

The two paths from the origin to the load have different lengths and therefore different impedances.

The shorter path has lower resistance.

More current therefore flows through the shorter path.

The longer path carries less current.

Current division follows the relative impedances of the two routes.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{ring current is not automatically shared equally}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 43 — Why Spread Large Loads Around a Ring?
questions.question: **Explain why large loads should not all be concentrated close together at one end of a ring final circuit. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Concentrating large loads at one location can produce unequal current sharing.

One leg may carry a disproportionately large current for a long period.

This can undermine the design assumption behind the ring-final-circuit overload arrangement.

Good circuit design therefore considers:

- load magnitude;
- load position;
- likely simultaneous demand.

Where large fixed loads are expected, separate dedicated circuits may be preferable.

---

questions.title: Question 44 — What Is a Spur?
questions.question: **Define a spur from a ring final circuit. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Formal BS 7671 definition

The uploaded Part 2 defines a **Spur** as:

> **“A branch from a ring or radial final circuit.”**

A spur therefore leaves the main circuit and does not itself continue as part of the main ring.

Conceptually:

\[
\text{ring point}\rightarrow\text{spur cable}\rightarrow\text{accessory}
\]

Spurs may be:

- unfused;
- fused through a suitable fused connection unit.

The permitted arrangement depends on the applicable design guidance and protective conditions.

---

questions.title: Question 45 — Unfused Spur
questions.question: Under the common BS 1363 ring-final guidance, what may an unfused spur normally supply? **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
An unfused spur is normally arranged to supply one:

- single socket-outlet;
- double socket-outlet;
- or one item of permanently connected equipment/accessory as permitted by the guidance.

The essential reason is that the spur cable is not protected by two ring paths.

Its loading must therefore be limited so that the spur conductor is not overloaded.

---

questions.title: Question 46 — Fused Spur
questions.question: **Explain the advantage of using a fused connection unit to supply a spur. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 47 — Spur from a Spur
questions.question:
A student proposes to take an unfused spur from another unfused spur.

**Explain why this is generally unacceptable in the standard ring-final arrangement. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
The first spur cable is already outside the current-sharing ring.

Adding further unfused sockets from that spur could allow multiple loads to be supplied through one 2.5 mm² branch while the branch remains protected only by the 30/32 A ring protective device.

This can overload the spur cable.

If multiple downstream outlets are required, a properly designed fused spur or separate circuit should be considered.

The key principle is:

\[
\boxed{\text{the branch cable must have appropriate overload protection}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 48 — Advantages of a Radial Circuit
questions.question: **State four advantages of radial final circuits. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 49 — Disadvantage of a Radial Circuit
questions.question: **State three possible disadvantages of a radial circuit compared with a ring arrangement for the same area/load. (3 marks)**

questions.title: Question 50 — Radial Circuit Open Line
questions.question:
A radial circuit supplies sockets A, B, C and D in that order.

The line conductor becomes open between B and C.

Which outlets are likely to remain operational? **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Sockets before the open point remain supplied:

\[
\boxed{A\text{ and }B}
\]

Sockets after the open point lose the line supply:

\[
\boxed{C\text{ and }D}
\]

This characteristic can assist fault location.

---

questions.title: Question 51 — Radial Circuit Open Neutral
questions.question:
The neutral conductor opens between B and C.

What symptom is expected at C and D? **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
C and D no longer have a complete normal return path.

Therefore connected appliances will normally fail to operate.

Depending on connected loads and test instruments, unusual or induced/back-fed voltage readings may still appear.

A broken neutral must therefore be diagnosed with proper voltage and continuity testing rather than assuming “no operation means no voltage.”

---

questions.title: Question 52 — 30 mA RCD Principle
questions.question: Under Brown Book Regulation 411.3.3, what rated residual operating current is used for additional protection of the relevant socket-outlets rated not exceeding 32 A? **(3 marks)**

questions.title: Question 53 — Why RCD Protection Is Valuable at Socket-Outlets
questions.question: **Explain why socket-outlets often require additional RCD protection. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 54 — Is There a Fixed Maximum Number of Sockets?
questions.question:
A student says:

> “A ring circuit is allowed exactly 10 sockets.”

Is this a sound design rule? Explain. **(5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 55 — Kitchen Circuit Planning
questions.question: **Why may a kitchen require special consideration rather than simply extending an existing general socket circuit? (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 56 — Fixed High-Power Load
questions.question:
A permanently connected 3 kW appliance is located beside a general-purpose socket circuit.

**Why might a dedicated circuit be preferable? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 57 — Current BS 7671 Conductor Colours
questions.answer:
Under the current harmonized BS 7671 identification system:

### Single-phase line

\[
\boxed{\text{Brown}}
\]

### Neutral

\[
\boxed{\text{Blue}}
\]

### Protective conductor

\[
\boxed{\text{Green-and-yellow}}
\]

### Three-phase

- L1:

\[
\boxed{\text{Brown}}
\]

- L2:

\[
\boxed{\text{Black}}
\]

- L3:

\[
\boxed{\text{Grey}}
\]

These are BS 7671/UK harmonized identification examples. Where EPRA asks specifically for Kenyan statutory colour requirements, answer according to the applicable Kenyan standard/code.

---

questions.title: Question 58 — Switched-Line Identification
questions.question:
A blue-insulated core is used as a switched line in a multicore lighting cable.

**What must be done? Explain. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
If a conductor colour normally associated with neutral is used as a line conductor in an allowed cable arrangement, it must be clearly identified at its terminations as a line conductor.

Under the harmonized system, suitable brown identification/sleeving is used.

The reason is to prevent someone later assuming that the conductor is neutral.

Correct conductor identification is a fundamental safety requirement.

---

questions.title: Question 59 — Protective Conductor Identification
questions.question: **How should a protective conductor be identified? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
A protective conductor is identified by:

\[
\boxed{\text{green-and-yellow}}
\]

This colour combination is reserved for protective-conductor identification.

A bare CPC in a cable is normally sleeved green-and-yellow at terminations.

---

questions.title: Question 60 — Socket Polarity
questions.question: **State the correct conductor functions that must be connected to the line, neutral and earth terminals of a socket-outlet. (3 marks)**

questions.title: Question 61 — Why Reverse Socket Polarity Is Dangerous
questions.question:
A socket has line and neutral reversed.

The appliance still works.

**Explain why the circuit is still unsafe. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 62 — Lighting Polarity
questions.question: **What does correct polarity mean in a one-way lighting circuit? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 63 — One-Way Lighting Continuity Test
questions.question: **Describe a dead-test method that can verify the line path and CPC at a one-way lighting point. (7 marks)**

questions.title: Question 64 — Two-Way Continuity Fault
questions.question:
A two-way lighting circuit passes continuity in one switch combination but fails in another.

**What does this suggest? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 65 — Ring End-to-End Results
questions.question:
A ring final circuit gives:

\[
r_1=0.82\Omega,\quad r_n=0.81\Omega,\quad r_2=1.35\Omega
\]

Are the results broadly plausible for a ring using equal-sized line/neutral conductors and a smaller CPC? Explain. **(6 marks)**
questions.answer:
Yes.

Line and neutral are expected to be similar because they normally have:

- same material;
- same CSA;
- same route length.

Therefore:

\[
0.82\Omega\approx0.81\Omega
\]

is reasonable.

The CPC is often smaller in CSA, so its resistance is higher:

\[
1.35\Omega>0.82\Omega
\]

The pattern is therefore plausible.

The result must still be compared with:

- expected conductor values;
- circuit length;
- actual cable construction.

---

questions.title: Question 66 — Open Ring Line
Question 67 — One Socket Gives High \(R_1+R_2\)
questions.question:
During ring crossover testing, most sockets give approximately:

\[
0.55\Omega
\]

One gives:

\[
1.20\Omega
\]

**State four possible causes. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 68 — Lamp Trips MCB Immediately
questions.question:
A lighting circuit MCB trips immediately every time one particular switch is turned ON.

**What type of faults should be suspected? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 69 — RCD Trips When Outdoor Lamp Is Switched On
questions.question:
A lighting circuit MCB remains ON, but the 30 mA RCD trips when an outdoor luminaire is energized.

**What faults are likely? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 70 — Socket MCB Trips Only with Appliance Connected
questions.question:
A socket circuit operates normally until one particular appliance is plugged in and switched ON.

**How should the fault be approached? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 71 — Socket Has L-E Voltage but No L-N Voltage
questions.question:
At a socket:

\[
L-E\approx230V
\]

but:

\[
L-N\approx0V
\]

with a load connected.

What conductor fault should be suspected first? **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
A likely fault is:

\[
\boxed{\text{open or high-resistance neutral}}
\]

The line conductor is present because line-to-Earth voltage is normal.

But the normal neutral return path is missing.

Further testing should confirm:

- neutral continuity;
- neutral-to-Earth voltage;
- upstream neutral connections.

---

questions.title: Question 72 — Socket Has No L-E but L-N Is Normal
questions.question:
A socket gives approximately:

\[
L-N=230V
\]

but:

\[
L-E\approx0V
\]

and CPC continuity is absent.

**What is the likely problem and why is it serious? (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
The likely fault is:

\[
\boxed{\text{broken or disconnected CPC}}
\]

Normal operation can continue because line and neutral are intact.

However, the socket has lost its protective earth connection.

If Class I equipment develops a line-to-case fault:

- the metal case may become live;
- fault current may be insufficient;
- protective disconnection may fail or be delayed.

The socket must not be accepted until protective continuity is restored.

---

questions.title: Question 73 — Two Sockets Dead on a Radial
questions.question:
A radial circuit has six socket-outlets.

Sockets 1–4 work.

Sockets 5–6 are dead.

**Where should fault-finding begin? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 74 — All Ring Sockets Work but Test Fails
questions.question:
Every socket on a ring final circuit supplies appliances normally.

End-to-end line continuity is open circuit.

**Can the ring be accepted? Explain. (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

The circuit is not operating as a complete ring.

It may have become two radials fed from the same 30/32 A protective device.

This can invalidate the overload assumptions of Regulation 433.1.204.

The fault must be located and repaired.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{functional operation is not proof of correct ring topology}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 75 — Design a Simple One-Way Lighting Circuit
questions.question:
A room requires one ceiling luminaire controlled from one wall switch.

**Describe the conductor functions and circuit operation from the distribution board to the lamp. (10 marks)**
questions.answer:
A suitable design contains:

### Supply

The final lighting circuit originates at a correctly selected protective device.

### Permanent line

Line is taken to the switching arrangement.

### Switch

The one-way switch receives permanent line at the appropriate common/input terminal.

When closed, the switch sends line potential along the switched-line conductor.

### Switched line

The switched line connects the switch output to the line terminal of the luminaire.

### Neutral

Neutral runs to the luminaire to complete the normal load-current path.

### CPC

The CPC runs continuously with the circuit and is connected to exposed metal parts requiring protective earthing.

### Operation

Switch ON:

\[
\text{line}\rightarrow\text{switch}\rightarrow\text{switched line}\rightarrow\text{lamp}\rightarrow\text{neutral}
\]

Switch OFF:

\[
\text{line path opened}
\]

so no normal load current flows through the lamp.

The switch must not be treated as a means of safe isolation for electrical work.

---

questions.title: Question 76 — Design a Three-Point Lighting Control
questions.answer:
Use:

- two-way switch at entrance A;
- intermediate switch at middle;
- two-way switch at entrance B.

Permanent line enters the COM of the first two-way switch.

The two strapper conductors pass from:

\[
L1,L2
\]

through the intermediate switch.

The intermediate switch either:

- passes strappers straight through;
- or crosses them.

The two strappers then reach L1/L2 of the second two-way switch.

The COM of the final two-way switch provides the switched line to the luminaire.

Neutral goes directly to the luminaire.

CPC continuity is maintained throughout.

Operating **any** of the three switches changes the lamp state.

---

questions.title: Question 77 — Compare Ring and Radial Socket Circuits
questions.answer:
### (a) Conductor path

Radial:

\[
\text{origin}\rightarrow\text{outlets}\rightarrow\text{end}
\]

Ring:

\[
\text{origin}\rightarrow\text{outlets}\rightarrow\text{return to origin}
\]

### (b) Load current

Radial conductors carry downstream load current.

Ring current divides between the two available paths according to load position and impedance.

### (c) Continuity faults

A radial open circuit normally disconnects downstream loads.

A ring open conductor may leave every outlet operational while destroying the intended ring arrangement.

### (d) Testing

Radial circuits require continuity/polarity tests appropriate to the circuit.

Ring circuits require special end-to-end and crossover continuity testing.

### (e) Overload design

A radial cable is normally coordinated directly with its protective device.

The common BS 1363 ring-final arrangement uses the special Regulation 433.1.204 conditions allowing a 30/32 A device with suitable ring conductors and load distribution.

---

questions.title: Question 78 — Ring Final Scenario
questions.question:
A 32 A BS 1363 ring final circuit is wired in 2.5 mm² copper cable.

The installation conditions reduce the cable current-carrying capacity of each leg to:

\[
17A
\]

Can the circuit simply be accepted because it is a ring? Explain. **(7 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

Regulation 433.1.204 requires the cable current-carrying capacity for the normal specified arrangement to be at least:

\[
\boxed{20A}
\]

The installed capacity is only:

\[
17A
\]

Therefore the normal deemed-to-comply ring arrangement cannot simply be claimed.

Possible design actions include:

- improve installation conditions;
- select larger conductors;
- reduce protective-device rating where correctly designed;
- redesign as suitable radial circuits;
- otherwise demonstrate full compliance by an appropriate engineering design.

The word “ring” does not automatically make an undersized cable safe.

---

questions.title: Question 79 — Lighting Oral Question
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“Explain one-way, two-way and intermediate switching without drawing.”**

Give a complete oral answer. **(12 marks)**
questions.answer:
### One-way

One switch controls a lamp from one position.

The switch opens or closes the line path between permanent line and switched line.

### Two-way

One lamp is controlled from two positions.

Two changeover switches are used.

Each has:

- COM;
- L1;
- L2.

Two strapper conductors connect the alternative paths between the switches.

Permanent line enters the common of one switch.

The common of the other provides switched line to the lamp.

Operating either switch changes which strapper path is selected and therefore reverses the lamp state.

### Intermediate

For control from three or more positions:

- use two-way switches at the two ends;
- place one or more intermediate switches between them.

An intermediate switch either:

- passes the strapper paths straight through;
- or crosses them.

Therefore operating any switch changes the continuity path and changes the lamp state.

Throughout the installation:

- neutral goes to the load as required;
- CPC continuity is maintained;
- switching is applied to the line conductor;
- conductors are correctly identified.

---

questions.title: Question 80 — Socket-Circuit Oral Question
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“How would you decide whether to use a radial or ring circuit for socket-outlets?”**

Give a strong answer. **(12 marks)**

title: Three-phase systems & motors
sourceTitle: Step 6 — Three-Phase Systems, Star/Delta Connections, Three-Phase Power, Motors, Motor Starting, Protection, Speed Control and Power Factor — Strengthened Distinction Edition

questions.title: Question 1 — What Is a Three-Phase Supply?
questions.question: **Define a three-phase AC supply. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A three-phase AC supply consists of three alternating voltages of the same:

- frequency;
- nominal magnitude;

but displaced in phase from one another by:

\[
\boxed{120^\circ}
\]

The three phases are commonly identified as:

\[
\boxed{L1,\quad L2,\quad L3}
\]

A neutral conductor may also be present depending on the system and connected loads.

The 120° displacement is what gives a balanced three-phase system its characteristic power-transfer and rotating-field advantages.

---

questions.title: Question 2 — Why 120 Degrees?
questions.question: **Explain why the phase displacement in a balanced three-phase system is 120°. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
One complete AC cycle is:

\[
360^\circ
\]

A three-phase system divides the cycle equally among three phases.

Therefore:

\[
\frac{360^\circ}{3}=120^\circ
\]

Hence the three phase voltages are separated by:

\[
\boxed{120^\circ}
\]

This equal spacing helps create a smooth transfer of power and a rotating magnetic field in three-phase motors.

---

questions.title: Question 3 — Identify the Conductors
questions.answer:
### L1, L2 and L3

These are the three line conductors carrying the three phase voltages.

They are displaced from each other by:

\[
120^\circ
\]

### Neutral

The neutral conductor is connected to the neutral point of the system and provides a return path for unbalanced single-phase currents where required.

In a perfectly balanced three-phase load:

\[
\boxed{I_N\approx0}
\]

because the three phase currents cancel vectorially.

In a real installation with unbalanced single-phase loads, neutral current may be present.

---

questions.title: Question 4 — Why Some Three-Phase Motors Do Not Need Neutral
questions.question: **Explain why many three-phase motors are supplied by L1, L2, L3 and CPC only, with no neutral. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A balanced three-phase motor uses current flowing between the three line conductors.

Its windings are connected in:

- star;
- or delta.

The motor does not normally require a neutral return path because the three phase currents form a balanced three-phase system.

Therefore many motors are supplied by:

\[
\boxed{L1,\ L2,\ L3,\ CPC}
\]

with no neutral conductor.

Control circuits may still require a neutral depending on their design.

---

questions.title: Question 5 — Advantages of Three-Phase Supply
questions.question: **State six advantages or uses of three-phase supply. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 6 — Define Line Voltage
questions.question: **Define line voltage in a three-phase system. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
Line voltage is the voltage measured:

\[
\boxed{\text{between any two line conductors}}
\]

For example:

\[
V_{L1-L2},\quad V_{L2-L3},\quad V_{L3-L1}
\]

Its symbol is often:

\[
V_L
\]

---

questions.title: Question 7 — Define Phase Voltage
questions.question: **Define phase voltage. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
Phase voltage is the voltage across one phase winding or one phase of the load.

Its symbol is commonly:

\[
V_{ph}
\]

In a star-connected system with neutral available, phase voltage is also the line-to-neutral voltage.

---

questions.title: Question 8 — Star Voltage Relationship
questions.question: **State the relationship between line voltage and phase voltage in a balanced star-connected system. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
For star:

\[
\boxed{V_L=\sqrt{3}V_{ph}}
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{V_{ph}=\frac{V_L}{\sqrt{3}}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 9 — Calculate Star Phase Voltage
questions.question:
A balanced star-connected load is supplied at:

\[
V_L=400V
\]

Calculate the phase voltage. **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{V_L}{\sqrt{3}}
\]

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{400}{1.732}
\]

\[
V_{ph}=230.95V
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{V_{ph}\approx231V}
\]

This explains why a 400/230 V three-phase system provides approximately 230 V line-to-neutral.

---

questions.title: Question 10 — Delta Voltage Relationship
questions.question: **State the line/phase voltage relationship in a delta-connected load. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
In delta:

\[
\boxed{V_L=V_{ph}}
\]

Each phase winding is connected directly between two line conductors.

Therefore each winding receives the full line voltage.

---

questions.title: Question 11 — Star Current Relationship
questions.question: **State the line/phase current relationship in a star-connected load. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
In star:

\[
\boxed{I_L=I_{ph}}
\]

The line conductor carries the same current as the phase winding to which it is connected.

---

questions.title: Question 12 — Delta Current Relationship
questions.question: **State the line/phase current relationship in a balanced delta-connected load. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
In delta:

\[
\boxed{I_L=\sqrt{3}I_{ph}}
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{I_{ph}=\frac{I_L}{\sqrt{3}}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 13 — Calculate Delta Phase Current
questions.question:
A delta-connected load draws:

\[
I_L=30A
\]

Calculate phase current. **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
I_{ph}=\frac{I_L}{\sqrt{3}}
\]

\[
I_{ph}=\frac{30}{1.732}
\]

\[
I_{ph}=17.32A
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{I_{ph}\approx17.3A}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 14 — Three-Phase Real Power Formula
questions.question: **State the formula for real power in a balanced three-phase system. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 15 — Three-Phase Apparent Power
questions.question: **State the formula for apparent power in a balanced three-phase system. (3 marks)**

questions.title: Question 16 — Three-Phase Reactive Power
questions.question: **State the formula for reactive power in a balanced three-phase system. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
\[
\boxed{Q=\sqrt{3}V_LI_L\sin\phi}
\]

where:

- \(Q\) = reactive power in var;
- \(\phi\) = phase angle between voltage and current.

---

questions.title: Question 17 — Calculate Three-Phase Power
questions.question:
A balanced three-phase load operates at:

\[
V_L=400V
\]

\[
I_L=25A
\]

\[
PF=0.8
\]

Calculate real power. **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
P=\sqrt{3}V_LI_L\cos\phi
\]

\[
P=1.732\times400\times25\times0.8
\]

\[
P=13856W
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{P\approx13.86kW}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 18 — Calculate Line Current
questions.question:
A three-phase motor takes:

\[
P=15kW
\]

from a:

\[
400V
\]

supply at:

\[
PF=0.82
\]

Ignoring efficiency for this question, calculate line current. **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
P=\sqrt{3}V_LI_LPF
\]

Rearrange:

\[
I_L=\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_LPF}
\]

Substitute:

\[
I_L=\frac{15000}{1.732\times400\times0.82}
\]

\[
I_L=26.40A
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{I_L\approx26.4A}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 19 — Include Motor Efficiency
questions.question:
A motor delivers:

\[
15kW
\]

mechanical output.

Efficiency is:

\[
\eta=90\%
\]

Power factor is:

\[
0.82
\]

Supply voltage:

\[
400V
\]

Calculate approximate line current. **(7 marks)**
questions.answer:
The electrical input power is greater than mechanical output power.

\[
\eta=\frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}
\]

Therefore:

\[
P_{in}=\frac{P_{out}}{\eta}
\]

Convert:

\[
90\%=0.90
\]

\[
P_{in}=\frac{15000}{0.90}
\]

\[
P_{in}=16666.7W
\]

Now:

\[
I_L=\frac{P_{in}}{\sqrt{3}V_LPF}
\]

\[
I_L=\frac{16666.7}{1.732\times400\times0.82}
\]

\[
I_L=29.34A
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{I_L\approx29.3A}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 20 — Balanced Three-Phase Load
questions.question: **What is meant by a balanced three-phase load? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A balanced three-phase load has substantially equal:

- phase impedances;
- phase currents;
- power factors

on all three phases.

The three currents are equal in magnitude and displaced by:

\[
120^\circ
\]

In a balanced four-wire system:

\[
\boxed{I_N\approx0}
\]

because the phase currents cancel vectorially in the neutral.

---

questions.title: Question 21 — Unbalanced Load
questions.question: **What is an unbalanced three-phase load? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 22 — Why Balance Single-Phase Loads?
questions.question: **Explain why single-phase loads in a three-phase installation should be distributed across the phases. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 23 — Define Phase Sequence
questions.question: **What is phase sequence? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Phase sequence is the order in which the three phase voltages reach corresponding positions in their AC cycles.

A normal sequence may be:

\[
\boxed{L1\rightarrow L2\rightarrow L3}
\]

The sequence matters for equipment such as three-phase motors.

---

questions.title: Question 24 — Reversing Two Phases
questions.question: **What happens to a three-phase motor if any two supply phases are interchanged? Explain. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Interchanging any two phases reverses the phase sequence.

The rotating magnetic field therefore reverses direction.

As a result, the motor generally rotates in the opposite direction.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{\text{swap any two phases}\rightarrow\text{reverse motor direction}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 25 — Describe Star Connection
questions.question: **Describe a star-connected three-phase load. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
In a star connection:

- one end of each of the three phase windings is joined at a common star point;
- the other end of each winding is connected to L1, L2 or L3.

The important relationships are:

\[
V_L=\sqrt{3}V_{ph}
\]

and:

\[
I_L=I_{ph}
\]

If the star point is brought out, it can form a neutral connection.

---

questions.title: Question 26 — Describe Delta Connection
questions.question: **Describe a delta-connected three-phase load. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 27 — Compare Winding Voltage
questions.question:
A motor is connected first in star and then in delta to the same line voltage.

**Compare the voltage across each winding. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
In star:

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{V_L}{\sqrt{3}}
\]

In delta:

\[
V_{ph}=V_L
\]

Therefore each winding receives a lower voltage in star.

For a 400 V supply:

Star winding voltage:

\[
\frac{400}{1.732}\approx231V
\]

Delta winding voltage:

\[
400V
\]

Thus the star winding voltage is approximately:

\[
\boxed{58\%}
\]

of the delta winding voltage.

---

questions.title: Question 28 — Principle of a Three-Phase Induction Motor
questions.question: **Explain the operating principle of a three-phase induction motor. (8 marks)**

questions.title: Question 29 — Why the Rotor Cannot Reach Synchronous Speed
questions.question: **Why does a standard induction motor rotor normally run below synchronous speed? (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
Rotor current is produced by electromagnetic induction.

For induction to occur, there must be relative motion between:

- the rotating stator field;
- the rotor.

If the rotor reached exactly the same speed as the rotating field:

\[
\boxed{\text{relative speed}=0}
\]

Therefore:

- no induced rotor EMF;
- no rotor current;
- no electromagnetic torque.

The rotor must therefore run slightly below synchronous speed.

The difference is called:

\[
\boxed{\text{slip}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 30 — Synchronous Speed Formula
questions.question: **State the synchronous-speed formula for an AC motor. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 31 — Calculate Synchronous Speed
questions.question:
A 4-pole motor is supplied at:

\[
50Hz
\]

Calculate synchronous speed. **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
\[
N_s=\frac{120f}{P}
\]

\[
N_s=\frac{120\times50}{4}
\]

\[
N_s=1500rpm
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{N_s=1500rpm}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 32 — Calculate Slip
questions.question:
A 4-pole 50 Hz induction motor runs at:

\[
1440rpm
\]

Calculate percentage slip. **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Synchronous speed:

\[
N_s=1500rpm
\]

Slip speed:

\[
N_s-N_r=1500-1440=60rpm
\]

Percentage slip:

\[
s=\frac{N_s-N_r}{N_s}\times100
\]

\[
s=\frac{60}{1500}\times100
\]

\[
\boxed{s=4\%}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 33 — Nameplate Information
questions.question: **State eight items commonly found on a three-phase motor nameplate. (8 marks)**

questions.title: Question 34 — Motor kW Rating
questions.question: **What does the kW rating on a motor nameplate normally represent? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The kW rating normally represents the rated:

\[
\boxed{\text{mechanical output power at the shaft}}
\]

under the specified operating conditions.

It is not automatically the electrical input power.

Because motor efficiency is less than 100%:

\[
P_{in}>P_{out}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 35 — Nameplate Current
questions.question: **Why is the motor nameplate current important? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 36 — Dual Voltage Nameplate
questions.question:
A motor nameplate shows:

\[
230/400V\quad \Delta/Y
\]

Explain the meaning. **(6 marks)**
questions.answer:
The motor windings are rated for approximately:

\[
230V
\]

each.

At a 230 V line supply:

- connect in delta;
- each winding receives 230 V.

At a 400 V line supply:

- connect in star;
- each winding receives:

\[
\frac{400}{\sqrt{3}}\approx230V
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{230V\ \Delta,\quad400V\ Y}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 37 — 400/690 V Motor
questions.question:
A motor nameplate shows:

\[
400/690V\quad \Delta/Y
\]

What connection is normally used on a 400 V supply? **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
At 400 V line voltage, the motor is intended to operate in:

\[
\boxed{\Delta}
\]

because each winding then receives:

\[
V_{ph}=V_L=400V
\]

At 690 V line voltage, it would be connected in star:

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{690}{1.732}\approx398V
\]

which is approximately the same winding voltage.

---

questions.title: Question 38 — Define DOL Starting
questions.question: **What is direct-on-line (DOL) starting? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 39 — Why DOL Current Is High
questions.question: **Explain why an induction motor draws a large current at starting. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 40 — DOL Advantages and Disadvantages
questions.question: **State three advantages and three disadvantages of DOL starting. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 41 — Purpose of Star-Delta Starting
questions.question: **What is the purpose of star-delta starting? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Star-delta starting reduces motor starting current by initially connecting the windings in:

\[
\boxed{\text{star}}
\]

The winding voltage is reduced to:

\[
\frac{V_L}{\sqrt{3}}
\]

After the motor accelerates, the windings are reconnected in:

\[
\boxed{\Delta}
\]

for normal running.

This reduces the electrical impact of starting compared with DOL.

---

questions.title: Question 42 — Starting Voltage in Star
questions.question:
A motor designed to run in delta at 400 V is started in star from a 400 V supply.

Calculate the voltage across each winding during starting. **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
In star:

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{V_L}{\sqrt{3}}
\]

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{400}{1.732}
\]

\[
V_{ph}=230.95V
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{V_{ph}\approx231V}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 43 — Starting Current Reduction
questions.question: **Approximately how does star connection affect starting current compared with delta for the same motor and supply? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Each winding receives:

\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
\]

of the delta winding voltage.

Winding current is therefore reduced.

The line current during star starting is approximately:

\[
\boxed{\frac{1}{3}}
\]

of the line current that would occur in delta at the same supply voltage, under the simplified starting comparison.

---

questions.title: Question 44 — Starting Torque Reduction
questions.question: **How is starting torque affected during star-delta starting? Explain. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Motor torque is approximately proportional to:

\[
V^2
\]

During star starting, winding voltage is reduced to:

\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
\]

of delta voltage.

Therefore torque becomes approximately:

\[
\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2
=
\frac{1}{3}
\]

Hence star starting torque is approximately:

\[
\boxed{\frac{1}{3}}
\]

of delta starting torque.

This makes star-delta unsuitable for loads requiring high starting torque.

---

questions.title: Question 45 — Star-Delta Suitability
questions.question: **State four conditions or considerations for using star-delta starting. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 46 — Reversing a Three-Phase Motor
questions.question: **How is the direction of a three-phase motor reversed? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
Reverse any two of the three phases.

For example:

\[
L1\leftrightarrow L2
\]

This reverses the phase sequence and therefore reverses the rotating magnetic field.

---

questions.title: Question 47 — Forward/Reverse Contactor Circuit
questions.question: **Why must forward and reverse contactors be interlocked? (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
The forward contactor applies one phase sequence.

The reverse contactor interchanges two phases.

If both contactors close simultaneously, phase conductors can be connected incorrectly against each other and produce a severe short circuit.

Therefore the circuit should use:

- electrical interlocking;
- and often mechanical interlocking.

The purpose is:

\[
\boxed{\text{prevent simultaneous forward and reverse contactor closure}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 48 — Three Different Motor Protection Functions
Question 49 — Why an Overload Relay Is Not a Short-Circuit Device
questions.question: **Explain why a motor overload relay does not replace short-circuit protection. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
An overload relay is designed to respond to sustained overcurrent associated with motor overload.

A short circuit can produce extremely high current requiring very rapid interruption and high breaking capacity.

The overload relay is not designed to interrupt large short-circuit fault current by itself.

Therefore motor circuits usually require separate:

- short-circuit protection;
- overload protection.

---

questions.title: Question 50 — Single Phasing
questions.question: **What is single phasing, and why is it dangerous to a three-phase motor? (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 51 — Locked Rotor
questions.question: **What is a locked-rotor condition, and why is it dangerous? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
A locked rotor occurs when the motor is energized but the rotor cannot turn.

Examples include:

- seized bearing;
- jammed machine;
- mechanically locked load.

The motor may draw current close to starting current continuously.

This produces rapid heating because the normal reduction in current after acceleration does not occur.

Overload protection should disconnect before thermal damage occurs.

---

questions.title: Question 52 — Factors Determining Induction-Motor Speed
questions.question: **State the two main electrical factors determining synchronous speed. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
From:

\[
N_s=\frac{120f}{P}
\]

synchronous speed depends on:

1. supply frequency \(f\);
2. number of poles \(P\).

---

questions.title: Question 53 — Variable Frequency Drive
questions.question: **Explain how a variable frequency drive (VFD) controls motor speed. (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
A VFD controls the frequency supplied to the motor.

Since:

\[
N_s=\frac{120f}{P}
\]

reducing frequency reduces synchronous speed.

Increasing frequency increases synchronous speed within the permitted operating range.

A VFD also controls voltage appropriately to maintain suitable motor magnetic flux.

Therefore VFDs provide:

- speed control;
- controlled acceleration/deceleration;
- reduced mechanical shock;
- possible energy savings in variable-torque loads.

---

questions.title: Question 54 — Why Voltage Alone Is Not Good Speed Control
questions.question: **Why is simply reducing voltage not an effective general method of controlling induction-motor speed? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Synchronous speed is primarily determined by:

\[
f
\]

and:

\[
P
\]

not by voltage.

Reducing voltage significantly:

- reduces available torque;
- increases slip under load;
- can increase heating;
- can cause stalling.

Therefore frequency control is the preferred general method for adjustable-speed induction motors.

---

questions.title: Question 55 — Define Power Factor
questions.question: **Define power factor. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Power factor is the ratio of real power to apparent power:

\[
\boxed{PF=\frac{P}{S}}
\]

For a sinusoidal system:

\[
\boxed{PF=\cos\phi}
\]

where \(\phi\) is the phase angle between voltage and current.

Power factor is dimensionless.

---

questions.title: Question 56 — Real, Reactive and Apparent Power
questions.question: **State the symbols and units of real, reactive and apparent power. (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Real Power

\[
P
\]

Unit:

\[
\boxed{W}
\]

### Reactive Power

\[
Q
\]

Unit:

\[
\boxed{var}
\]

### Apparent Power

\[
S
\]

Unit:

\[
\boxed{VA}
\]

Relationship:

\[
\boxed{S^2=P^2+Q^2}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 57 — Why Induction Motors Have Lagging Power Factor
questions.question: **Explain why induction motors normally have a lagging power factor. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
An induction motor requires magnetizing current to establish its magnetic field.

This magnetizing current is largely inductive.

In an inductive load:

\[
\boxed{\text{current lags voltage}}
\]

Therefore the motor draws reactive power in addition to real power.

This produces a lagging power factor below unity.

---

questions.title: Question 58 — Disadvantages of Poor Power Factor
questions.question: **State six disadvantages of poor power factor. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 59 — Current at Different Power Factors
questions.question:
A three-phase load requires:

\[
20kW
\]

at:

\[
400V
\]

Calculate current at:

**(a)** PF = 1.0  
**(b)** PF = 0.8.

**(8 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
I=\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_LPF}
\]

### (a) PF = 1

\[
I=\frac{20000}{1.732\times400\times1}
\]

\[
I=28.87A
\]

\[
\boxed{I\approx28.9A}
\]

### (b) PF = 0.8

\[
I=\frac{20000}{1.732\times400\times0.8}
\]

\[
I=36.09A
\]

\[
\boxed{I\approx36.1A}
\]

The poorer-power-factor load requires substantially more current for the same real power.

---

questions.title: Question 60 — Principle of Power-Factor Correction
questions.question: **Explain how capacitors improve the power factor of an inductive load. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 61 — Does PF Correction Reduce kW Load?
questions.question: **Does power-factor correction significantly reduce the real kW required by an unchanged motor load? Explain. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

The mechanical load still requires approximately the same real power.

Power-factor correction mainly reduces:

- reactive power drawn from the supply;
- apparent power;
- supply current.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{kW remains approximately unchanged}}
\]

while:

\[
kvar\downarrow,\quad kVA\downarrow,\quad I\downarrow
\]

---

questions.title: Question 62 — Power Triangle Calculation
questions.question:
A load has:

\[
P=30kW
\]

and:

\[
PF=0.75
\]

Calculate apparent power. **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
\[
PF=\frac{P}{S}
\]

Therefore:

\[
S=\frac{P}{PF}
\]

\[
S=\frac{30}{0.75}
\]

\[
\boxed{S=40kVA}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 63 — Calculate Reactive Power
questions.question:
Using Question 62:

\[
P=30kW,\qquad S=40kVA
\]

Calculate reactive power. **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
S^2=P^2+Q^2
\]

Therefore:

\[
Q=\sqrt{S^2-P^2}
\]

\[
Q=\sqrt{40^2-30^2}
\]

\[
Q=\sqrt{1600-900}
\]

\[
Q=\sqrt{700}
\]

\[
Q=26.46kvar
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{Q\approx26.5kvar}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 64 — Capacitor kvar Required
questions.question:
A 30 kW load operates at:

\[
PF_1=0.75
\]

It is to be corrected to:

\[
PF_2=0.95
\]

Calculate the required capacitor kvar. **(8 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
Q_c=P(\tan\phi_1-\tan\phi_2)
\]

First:

\[
\cos\phi_1=0.75
\]

\[
\phi_1=\cos^{-1}(0.75)
\]

\[
\phi_1\approx41.41^\circ
\]

\[
\tan\phi_1\approx0.882
\]

Now:

\[
\cos\phi_2=0.95
\]

\[
\phi_2=\cos^{-1}(0.95)
\]

\[
\phi_2\approx18.19^\circ
\]

\[
\tan\phi_2\approx0.329
\]

Therefore:

\[
Q_c=30(0.882-0.329)
\]

\[
Q_c=30\times0.553
\]

\[
Q_c=16.59kvar
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{Q_c\approx16.6kvar}
\]

A practical capacitor-bank size would be selected from available standard ratings and the actual system requirements.

---

questions.title: Question 65 — Current Before and After PF Correction
questions.question:
The 30 kW load in Question 64 is supplied at:

\[
400V
\]

Calculate line current:

**(a)** before correction at PF 0.75;  
**(b)** after correction at PF 0.95.

**(8 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
I=\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_LPF}
\]

### Before correction

\[
I_1=\frac{30000}{1.732\times400\times0.75}
\]

\[
I_1=57.74A
\]

\[
\boxed{I_1\approx57.7A}
\]

### After correction

\[
I_2=\frac{30000}{1.732\times400\times0.95}
\]

\[
I_2=45.58A
\]

\[
\boxed{I_2\approx45.6A}
\]

Current reduction:

\[
57.7-45.6=12.1A
\]

Therefore correction reduces the supply current substantially.

---

questions.title: Question 66 — Why Use Automatic PF Correction?
questions.question: **Why are automatic capacitor banks used in installations where load changes significantly? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
If the load changes, the reactive-power requirement also changes.

A fixed capacitor bank may then:

- under-correct at high load;
- over-correct at low load.

Automatic power-factor-correction equipment switches capacitor stages in and out according to the measured system condition.

This helps maintain the target power factor over changing load.

---

questions.title: Question 67 — Danger of Overcorrection
questions.question: **What is overcorrection of power factor, and why can it be undesirable? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 68 — Full Motor Input Calculation
questions.answer:
### (a) Input power

\[
\eta=\frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}
\]

Therefore:

\[
P_{in}=\frac{P_{out}}{\eta}
\]

\[
P_{in}=\frac{22000}{0.91}
\]

\[
P_{in}=24175.8W
\]

\[
\boxed{P_{in}\approx24.18kW}
\]

### (b) Line current

\[
I_L=\frac{P_{in}}{\sqrt{3}V_LPF}
\]

\[
I_L=\frac{24175.8}{1.732\times400\times0.84}
\]

\[
I_L=41.55A
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{I_L\approx41.6A}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 69 — Motor Nameplate Interpretation
questions.question:
A motor nameplate reads:

\[
400/690V\quad \Delta/Y
\]

\[
18.5kW,\quad 35A,\quad 50Hz,\quad 1470rpm,\quad PF=0.86
\]

Answer the following:

**(a)** connection on a 400 V supply;  
**(b)** synchronous speed if it is a four-pole motor;  
**(c)** approximate slip;  
**(d)** meaning of 18.5 kW;  
**(e)** meaning of PF 0.86.

**(12 marks)**
questions.answer:
### (a) Connection

For:

\[
400/690V\quad\Delta/Y
\]

at 400 V:

\[
\boxed{\Delta}
\]

---

### (b) Synchronous speed

\[
N_s=\frac{120f}{P}
\]

\[
N_s=\frac{120\times50}{4}
\]

\[
\boxed{N_s=1500rpm}
\]

---

### (c) Slip

\[
s=\frac{1500-1470}{1500}\times100
\]

\[
s=\frac{30}{1500}\times100
\]

\[
\boxed{s=2\%}
\]

---

### (d) 18.5 kW

This is approximately the rated mechanical shaft output power under rated operating conditions.

---

### (e) PF 0.86

The motor's real power is 86% of its apparent power ratio:

\[
PF=\frac{P}{S}=0.86
\]

The current lags voltage because the motor is predominantly inductive.

---

questions.title: Question 70 — Choose DOL or Star-Delta
questions.question:
A motor drives a pump that requires only moderate starting torque.

The supply network is sensitive to voltage dip.

Would DOL or star-delta be more suitable in principle, and why? **(6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 71 — High Starting Torque Load
questions.question:
A conveyor requires high torque immediately from rest.

Why may star-delta starting be unsuitable? **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Star-delta reduces winding voltage.

Since motor torque is approximately proportional to:

\[
V^2
\]

the starting torque is reduced to roughly:

\[
\boxed{\frac{1}{3}}
\]

of delta starting torque.

A high-torque load may therefore:

- fail to accelerate;
- remain at low speed;
- draw high current too long;
- overheat.

A different starting method may be required.

---

questions.title: Question 72 — Explain Star vs Delta Without Drawing
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“Explain the difference between star and delta connections.”**

Give a complete answer. **(10 marks)**

questions.title: Question 73 — Explain a Three-Phase Motor from Supply to Torque
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“Explain how three-phase electricity makes an induction motor turn.”**

Give a complete answer. **(12 marks)**
questions.answer:
1. Three-phase supply provides three currents displaced by 120°.
2. These currents flow in stator windings physically arranged around the motor.
3. Their magnetic fields combine to form a rotating magnetic field.
4. The rotating field cuts the rotor conductors.
5. Relative motion induces rotor EMF.
6. Rotor current flows because the rotor circuit is closed.
7. Rotor current produces a magnetic field.
8. The stator and rotor magnetic fields interact.
9. Electromagnetic torque is produced.
10. The rotor accelerates in the direction of the rotating field.
11. As speed rises, slip reduces.
12. The rotor settles at a speed slightly below synchronous speed where developed torque equals load torque.

Therefore the motor is called an:

\[
\boxed{\text{induction motor}}
\]

because rotor current is induced rather than directly supplied in the common squirrel-cage design.

---

questions.title: Question 74 — Explain Motor Protection
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“What protection does a three-phase motor require?”**

Give a strong answer. **(12 marks)**
questions.answer:
A motor installation may require protection against:

### 1. Short circuit

Very high fault current between live conductors.

Use suitable fuse/circuit-breaker with adequate breaking capacity.

### 2. Overload

Sustained excessive current due to mechanical overload or abnormal operation.

Use overload relay or suitable motor-protection device.

### 3. Earth fault

Fault from live conductor to exposed metalwork/Earth.

Requires protective earthing and appropriate fault-protection device.

### 4. Phase loss

Single phasing can overheat the motor.

Suitable protection should detect damaging phase-loss/unbalance conditions.

### 5. Locked rotor/stall

A stalled motor may draw high current continuously.

Protection should disconnect before thermal damage.

### 6. Undervoltage/restart considerations

Automatic unexpected restart after supply restoration may be dangerous.

Control circuits may use undervoltage release/no-volt protection.

### 7. Temperature

Large or critical motors may use winding or bearing temperature protection.

Protection must coordinate with:

- cable;
- starter;
- contactor;
- motor nameplate current;
- starting current;
- fault level.

---

questions.title: Question 75 — Explain Power Factor to an Examiner
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“What is power factor, why is poor power factor undesirable, and how do you correct it?”**

Give a complete answer. **(15 marks)**
questions.answer:
Power factor is:

\[
PF=\frac{P}{S}
\]

For a sinusoidal system:

\[
PF=\cos\phi
\]

Inductive loads such as motors require magnetizing current.

This causes current to lag voltage and produces reactive power.

For the same real power, a low power factor requires higher current.

Higher current causes:

- higher \(I^2R\) losses;
- greater voltage drop;
- larger cable requirements;
- greater transformer loading;
- greater generator loading;
- larger switchgear requirements;
- lower usable system capacity.

Power factor can be improved using capacitors.

Capacitors supply leading reactive current that offsets part of the lagging reactive current of inductive loads.

The correction does not significantly reduce the motor's required real kW.

It mainly reduces:

\[
Q,\quad S,\quad I
\]

A capacitor bank can be calculated using:

\[
\boxed{Q_c=P(\tan\phi_1-\tan\phi_2)}
\]

where:

- \(\phi_1\) = original phase angle;
- \(\phi_2\) = target phase angle.

For changing loads, automatic capacitor banks can switch stages in and out.

---

title: Diversity, instruments & safety
sourceTitle: Step 7 — Maximum Demand, Diversity, Utilization, Protection Selectivity, Measuring Instruments, Electrical Safety and First Aid — Strengthened Distinction Edition

questions.title: Question 1 — Define Connected Load
questions.question: **Define connected load. (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
Connected load is the total rated load of electrical equipment connected to an installation or circuit.

It is obtained by adding the rated powers of the connected equipment.

For example, if an installation contains:

- 2 kW heater;
- 3 kW cooker load;
- 1 kW water heater;

then:

\[
P_{\text{connected}}=2+3+1
\]

\[
\boxed{P_{\text{connected}}=6kW}
\]

Connected load does not necessarily mean all equipment will operate simultaneously at full rating.

---

questions.title: Question 2 — Define Maximum Demand
questions.question: **Define maximum demand. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 3 — Why Maximum Demand Matters
questions.question: **Give five reasons why maximum demand is important in electrical design. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 4 — Connected Load vs Maximum Demand
questions.question:
An installation has a connected load of:

\[
30kW
\]

but the estimated maximum demand is:

\[
18kW
\]

Explain why both figures can be correct. **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The connected load represents the total rating of all installed loads.
