The maximum demand represents the greatest load expected to operate simultaneously.

Therefore:

\[
30kW
\]

may be installed, but operating patterns may mean that the greatest simultaneous demand is only:

\[
18kW
\]

This is normal and is the reason diversity is considered in electrical design.

---

questions.title: Question 5 — Define Demand Factor
questions.question: **Define demand factor and give its formula. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 6 — Calculate Demand Factor
questions.question:
An installation has:

\[
P_{\text{connected}}=40kW
\]

and:

\[
P_{\text{max demand}}=28kW
\]

Calculate the demand factor. **(4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 7 — Define Diversity Factor
questions.question: **Define diversity factor and give its formula. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 8 — Diversity Factor Calculation
questions.question:
Three sections of an installation have individual maximum demands of:

\[
10kW,\quad15kW,\quad20kW
\]

The maximum demand measured for the whole installation is:

\[
30kW
\]

Calculate the diversity factor. **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Sum of individual maximum demands:

\[
10+15+20=45kW
\]

Therefore:

\[
\text{Diversity Factor}=\frac{45}{30}
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{Diversity Factor}=1.5}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 9 — Why Diversity Factor Exceeds 1
questions.question: **Explain why diversity factor is normally greater than 1. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The maximum demand of every individual load or section usually occurs at different times.

Therefore the sum of their individual peaks is greater than the maximum simultaneous demand of the whole installation.

Hence:

\[
\frac{\sum \text{individual peaks}}
{\text{simultaneous system peak}}
>1
\]

This is the basic principle of diversity.

---

questions.title: Question 10 — Diversity Does Not Mean Guessing
questions.question: **Explain why diversity should not be applied as an arbitrary percentage without considering the installation. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 11 — Define Utilization Factor
questions.question: **Define utilization factor in an electrical-system design context. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 12 — Utilization-Factor Calculation
questions.question:
A distribution transformer is rated at:

\[
100kVA
\]

The highest demand is:

\[
72kVA
\]

Calculate utilization factor. **(4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 13 — Distinguish Demand, Diversity and Utilization
questions.question: **Differentiate between demand factor, diversity factor and utilization factor. (9 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Demand Factor

\[
\frac{\text{maximum demand}}
{\text{connected load}}
\]

Normally:

\[
\leq1
\]

---

### Diversity Factor

\[
\frac{\sum\text{individual maximum demands}}
{\text{maximum simultaneous demand}}
\]

Normally:

\[
>1
\]

---

### Utilization Factor

A common system-design definition is:

\[
\frac{\text{maximum demand}}
{\text{rated equipment/system capacity}}
\]

Normally:

\[
\leq1
\]

These three terms describe different relationships and should not be used interchangeably.

---

questions.title: Question 14 — Basic Maximum-Demand Calculation
questions.answer:
\[
P_{MD}=2.5+5.0+3.0+4.5
\]

\[
\boxed{P_{MD}=15.0kW}
\]

The figures supplied are already diversified values, so they are added directly.

---

questions.title: Question 15 — Single-Phase Current from Maximum Demand
questions.question:
Using Question 14, assume:

\[
V=230V
\]

and unity power factor.

Calculate the design current corresponding to the 15 kW maximum demand. **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
\[
I=\frac{P}{V}
\]

\[
I=\frac{15000}{230}
\]

\[
I=65.22A
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{I\approx65.2A}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 16 — Three-Phase Current from Maximum Demand
questions.question:
A balanced three-phase installation has an estimated maximum demand of:

\[
45kW
\]

at:

\[
400V
\]

and:

\[
PF=0.9
\]

Calculate line current. **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Use:

\[
P=\sqrt{3}V_LI_LPF
\]

Therefore:

\[
I_L=\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_LPF}
\]

\[
I_L=\frac{45000}{1.732\times400\times0.9}
\]

\[
I_L=72.17A
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{I_L\approx72.2A}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 17 — Define Selectivity
questions.question: **Define protection selectivity or discrimination. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Formal BS 7671 definition

The uploaded Part 2 uses **Selectivity** by reference to **Discrimination**, which it defines as:

> **“Ability of a protective device to operate in preference to another protective device in series.”**

In practical coordination terms, selectivity means arranging protective devices so that the device nearest the fault operates while upstream devices remain closed where possible.

The goal is:

\[
\boxed{\text{disconnect the smallest necessary part of the installation}}
\]

This improves:

- continuity of supply;
- fault localization;
- operational reliability.

---

questions.title: Question 18 — Why Selectivity Matters
questions.question: **State five advantages of good protective-device selectivity. (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 19 — Selective Operation Example
questions.question:
A final circuit MCB and an upstream main breaker both trip for a small fault on one socket circuit.

**Why may this indicate poor selectivity? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Ideally, the final-circuit protective device should clear a fault that is within its protective zone.

If the upstream main breaker also trips unnecessarily:

- unrelated circuits lose supply;
- fault localization is poorer;
- continuity of service is reduced.

This can indicate that the time/current characteristics of the two devices are not adequately coordinated for that fault level.

---

questions.title: Question 20 — Total vs Partial Selectivity
questions.question: **Differentiate between total selectivity and partial selectivity. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Total Selectivity

The downstream protective device operates alone for all fault currents up to the maximum prospective fault current at the protected point.

### Partial Selectivity

The downstream device operates alone only up to a specified fault-current level.

Above that level, the upstream device may also operate.

Therefore selectivity is not always an all-or-nothing condition.

---

questions.title: Question 21 — Time Selectivity
questions.question: **Explain the principle of time selectivity. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Time selectivity uses intentional differences in operating time.

The downstream protective device is arranged to operate faster.

The upstream device has a delay for fault currents within the coordinated range.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{downstream device clears first}}
\]

while the upstream device remains closed unless the downstream device fails or the fault lies outside its zone.

---

questions.title: Question 22 — Current Selectivity
questions.question: **Explain the principle of current selectivity. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Current selectivity relies on different operating-current thresholds.

The downstream device is set or selected to respond at a lower current than the upstream device.

For certain fault-current ranges:

- downstream device operates;
- upstream device remains closed.

Actual selectivity should be confirmed using manufacturer data or coordination tables rather than assumed only from device ampere ratings.

---

questions.title: Question 23 — RCD Selectivity
questions.question: **How can RCDs be arranged to improve selectivity? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Selectivity can be improved by coordinating:

- rated residual operating current;
- operating time;
- device type.

For example, an upstream time-delayed/selective RCD may be coordinated with downstream general RCDs so that the downstream device operates first for a local residual-current fault.

Correct coordination depends on the applicable system and manufacturer data.

---

questions.title: Question 24 — Why Ratings Alone Are Not Enough
questions.question:
A 100 A upstream breaker supplies a 32 A downstream breaker.

**Can you automatically conclude that the devices are selective? Explain. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 25 — Voltmeter
questions.question: **What does a voltmeter measure, and how is it connected? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A voltmeter measures:

\[
\boxed{\text{potential difference}}
\]

in volts.

It is connected:

\[
\boxed{\text{in parallel}}
\]

across the two points between which voltage is required.

An ideal voltmeter has very high internal resistance so that it draws minimal current from the circuit being measured.

---

questions.title: Question 26 — Ammeter
questions.question: **What does an ammeter measure, and how is it connected? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
An ammeter measures:

\[
\boxed{\text{electric current}}
\]

in amperes.

A conventional ammeter is connected:

\[
\boxed{\text{in series}}
\]

with the circuit whose current is being measured.

It has very low internal resistance so that it introduces minimal voltage drop.

Connecting a low-resistance current input directly across a voltage source can cause a severe short circuit.

---

questions.title: Question 27 — Ohmmeter
questions.question: **What does an ohmmeter measure, and why should resistance normally be measured on a de-energized circuit? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
An ohmmeter measures electrical resistance.

It uses its own internal test source.

If connected to an energized circuit:

- external voltage can damage the instrument;
- the reading may be meaningless;
- the operator may be exposed to danger.

Therefore resistance testing is normally carried out on:

\[
\boxed{\text{safely isolated, proved-dead circuits}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 28 — Multimeter
questions.question: **State six quantities or functions a typical digital multimeter may provide. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 29 — Clamp Meter
questions.question: **Explain the main advantage of a clamp meter. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 30 — Why Clamp One Conductor?
questions.question:
A clamp meter is placed around both line and neutral of a healthy single-phase circuit.

What approximate reading should be expected, and why? **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
In a healthy circuit:

\[
I_L\approx I_N
\]

but the currents flow in opposite directions.

Their magnetic fields cancel.

Therefore the clamp should read approximately:

\[
\boxed{0A}
\]

A sensitive leakage-current clamp can use this principle to detect residual current where the cancellation is not exact.

---

questions.title: Question 31 — Low-Resistance Continuity Tester
questions.question: **What is a low-resistance continuity tester used for? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
It is used to measure low conductor resistances such as:

- CPC continuity;
- bonding continuity;
- \(R_1+R_2\);
- ring end-to-end resistance.

Results are commonly in:

\[
\Omega
\]

or:

\[
m\Omega
\]

It is designed for low-resistance measurement, unlike an insulation-resistance tester.

---

questions.title: Question 32 — Insulation-Resistance Tester
questions.question: **What is an insulation-resistance tester used for? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 33 — Earth-Fault Loop Tester
questions.question: **What does an earth-fault loop impedance tester measure? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
It measures the impedance of the earth-fault loop.

Depending on where and how it is used, it can determine values such as:

\[
Z_e
\]

or:

\[
Z_s
\]

The result helps establish whether sufficient fault current can flow to operate the protective device within the required time.

Because many loop tests are live tests, safe procedure is essential.

---

questions.title: Question 34 — RCD Tester
questions.question: **What does an RCD tester verify? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
An RCD tester applies a controlled residual current and measures the response of the RCD.

Depending on the test method and applicable standard, it may verify:

- operating time;
- residual-current response;
- correct disconnection.

It provides quantitative information that the integral RCD test button alone does not provide.

---

questions.title: Question 35 — Phase-Sequence Meter
questions.question: **What is a phase-sequence meter used for? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
It identifies the order of the three phases.

For example:

\[
L1\rightarrow L2\rightarrow L3
\]

It is useful when:

- commissioning three-phase installations;
- checking motor rotation arrangements;
- verifying consistent phase sequence.

---

questions.title: Question 36 — Earth-Electrode Resistance Tester
questions.question: **What is an earth-electrode resistance tester used for? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
It measures the resistance of an earth electrode or earthing system to the general mass of Earth using an appropriate test method.

It is particularly relevant to installations such as:

- TT systems;
- lightning protection;
- dedicated earthing systems.

Test method depends on site conditions and may use auxiliary test electrodes or suitable alternative techniques.

---

questions.title: Question 37 — Two-Pole Voltage Detector
questions.question: **Why is a two-pole voltage detector preferred for proving dead? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 38 — Proving Unit
questions.question: **What is the purpose of a proving unit? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A proving unit provides a known test voltage that confirms the voltage indicator is functioning.

It is used:

1. before proving the circuit dead;
2. after proving the circuit dead.

This confirms that a zero indication was not caused by instrument failure.

---

questions.title: Question 39 — Accuracy
questions.question: **What is instrument accuracy? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
Accuracy is the closeness of an instrument's indicated value to the true value.

An instrument with poor accuracy may give a repeatable reading that is still incorrect.

Accuracy is therefore different from repeatability.

---

questions.title: Question 40 — Resolution
questions.question: **What is instrument resolution? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
Resolution is the smallest change in the measured quantity that the instrument can display or distinguish.

For example, a meter displaying to:

\[
0.01V
\]

has finer voltage resolution than one displaying only to:

\[
0.1V
\]

within the relevant range.

---

questions.title: Question 41 — Calibration
questions.question: **Why is calibration or periodic accuracy verification important? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 42 — Wrong Multimeter Range
questions.question:
A technician attempts to measure a 230 V supply while the multimeter leads are connected to the high-current input terminals.

**Why is this dangerous? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 43 — CAT Rating
questions.question: **What is the purpose of an instrument measurement-category rating such as CAT II, CAT III or CAT IV? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Measurement categories relate to the transient-overvoltage environment in which test equipment is intended to be safely used.

Higher-energy parts of an electrical distribution system can expose instruments to larger transient currents and overvoltages.

The instrument must therefore have a category and voltage rating suitable for the point of measurement.

A small electronics multimeter may not be safe for measurements at a distribution board even if its display can show the nominal voltage.

---

questions.title: Question 44 — What Is Electric Shock?
questions.question: **Define electric shock. (3 marks)**

questions.title: Question 45 — Factors Affecting Shock Severity
questions.question: **State six factors that influence the severity of electric shock. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 46 — Why Wet Conditions Increase Risk
questions.question: **Explain why electric-shock risk generally increases in wet conditions. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Water, especially water containing dissolved salts or contaminants, reduces the effective resistance of the skin and contact path.

From:

\[
I=\frac{V}{R}
\]

if resistance falls while voltage remains the same:

\[
I\uparrow
\]

Therefore more current may pass through the body.

Wet conditions can also increase:

- contact area;
- contact with Earth;
- likelihood of conductive surfaces.

---

questions.title: Question 47 — Touch Voltage
questions.question: **What is touch voltage? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Touch voltage is the voltage that may appear between conductive parts that can be touched simultaneously, or between an exposed-conductive-part and Earth, during a fault.

For example, if a metal appliance case becomes energized because of a fault, a person touching:

- the case;
- and an earthed object or the ground

may be exposed to a dangerous potential difference.

---

questions.title: Question 48 — Step Potential
questions.question: **What is step potential? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 49 — Hierarchy: De-Energize First
questions.question: **Why should electrical work normally be carried out de-energized where practicable? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 50 — PPE Is Not a Substitute for Isolation
questions.question: **Explain why PPE should not be used as an excuse to work live unnecessarily. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 51 — Damaged Test Leads
questions.question: **Why should damaged meter leads never be used? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 52 — Working in a Wet Area
questions.question: **State six precautions relevant when electrical work is required in a wet or damp environment. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 53 — Causes of Electrical Fire
questions.question: **State six electrical faults or conditions that can cause fire. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 54 — Loose Connection Heating
questions.question: **Explain why a loose connection can overheat even when circuit current is not excessive. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
A loose connection can create high local resistance.

Power dissipated at the connection is:

\[
P=I^2R
\]

If local resistance rises:

\[
R\uparrow
\]

then heating rises for the same current.

The small connection area concentrates the heat.

This can:

- damage insulation;
- carbonize material;
- cause arcing;
- start a fire.

---

questions.title: Question 55 — Water on Energized Electrical Equipment
questions.question: **Why should ordinary water not be directed onto energized electrical equipment during a fire? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Water can conduct electrical current, particularly when contaminated.

Applying water to energized equipment can create:

- shock hazard;
- current paths through the user;
- additional short circuits.

The electrical supply should be isolated where safe to do so, and the correct firefighting method/equipment for the situation should be used.

Personal safety and emergency-service instructions take priority.

---

questions.title: Question 56 — First Action at an Electrical-Shock Scene
questions.question:
A person is still in contact with an energized conductor.

**What is the first priority? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
The first priority is:

\[
\boxed{\text{make the scene electrically safe without becoming another casualty}}
\]

Do **not** touch the person while they remain in contact with the energized source.

Where safe and practicable:

- switch off/isolate the electrical supply;
- have another person activate emergency services.

Only approach/touch the casualty when the electrical hazard has been removed or controlled.

---

questions.title: Question 57 — Why Not Grab the Casualty?
questions.question: **Why must you not simply grab a person who is still in contact with live electricity? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The casualty's body may be part of the electrical circuit.

Touching them can create a new path through the rescuer.

The rescuer may then also receive an electric shock.

This can produce:

\[
\boxed{\text{two casualties instead of one}}
\]

The source must be made safe first.

---

questions.title: Question 58 — Initial Casualty Assessment
questions.question: Once the electrical source is safely isolated, what should be assessed first? **(6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 59 — CPR Compression Rate
questions.question: For an adult in cardiac arrest, what chest-compression rate is recommended by current Red Cross guidance? **(3 marks)**
questions.answer:
The recommended rate is:

\[
\boxed{100\text{ to }120\text{ compressions per minute}}
\]

Compressions should be delivered on a firm, flat surface where possible.

Current CPR/AED training should be followed in a real emergency.

---

questions.title: Question 60 — CPR Compression-to-Breath Ratio
questions.question: For a trained rescuer providing standard adult CPR, what compression-to-breath pattern is commonly taught? **(3 marks)**

questions.title: Question 61 — AED
questions.question: **What is an AED and when should it be used? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
AED means:

\[
\boxed{\text{Automated External Defibrillator}}
\]

It analyzes the heart rhythm of a person in cardiac arrest and advises/delivers a shock when appropriate.

For an unresponsive person who is not breathing normally:

- CPR should begin;
- an AED should be obtained and used as soon as possible;
- follow the device voice/visual instructions.

No one should touch the casualty while the AED is analyzing or delivering a shock.

---

questions.title: Question 62 — Unresponsive but Breathing
questions.question:
An electrical-shock casualty is unresponsive but breathing normally after the source has been isolated.

**What general care is appropriate? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Activate emergency medical services.

Maintain:

- airway;
- breathing observation;
- body temperature.

If there is no suspected spinal/major trauma and the situation is appropriate, a recovery position can help maintain the airway.

Continue monitoring because the person's condition can deteriorate.

Electrical injuries require medical assessment even where external injuries appear minor.

---

questions.title: Question 63 — Why Electrical Burns Are Deceptive
questions.question: **Why can an electrical burn be more serious than it appears? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 64 — First Aid for an Electrical Burn
questions.question: After the source is safely isolated and the casualty is stable, state the general first-aid approach for an electrical burn. **(6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 65 — Why Medical Evaluation Is Important
questions.question:
A worker receives an electric shock and has only a tiny burn mark on one finger.

He says he feels fine.

**Why should the event not automatically be dismissed as minor? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 66 — Fallen Conductor
questions.question:
A person is lying near a fallen power conductor.

**Why is it dangerous to run directly toward the person? (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
The conductor may still be energized.

Current entering the ground can create a voltage gradient.

This produces:

\[
\boxed{\text{step potential}}
\]

between points on the ground.

A rescuer may receive current from one foot to the other.

The area should be treated as energized until the supply authority/emergency personnel make it safe.

The casualty should not be approached casually.

---

questions.title: Question 67 — Electrician Shocked on a Ladder
questions.question:
An electrician receives a shock while working on a ladder and falls.

The supply is isolated.

**Besides the electrical injury, what other injuries should be considered? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 68 — Person Appears Well After Shock
questions.question:
A worker receives a brief shock, remains conscious and says no treatment is needed.

**What should a competent supervisor do? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 69 — Select the Correct Instrument
questions.answer:
### (a)

\[
\boxed{\text{Two-pole voltage detector + proving unit}}
\]

### (b)

\[
\boxed{\text{Low-resistance continuity tester}}
\]

### (c)

\[
\boxed{\text{Insulation-resistance tester}}
\]

### (d)

\[
\boxed{\text{Clamp meter}}
\]

### (e)

\[
\boxed{\text{Earth-fault loop impedance tester}}
\]

### (f)

\[
\boxed{\text{RCD tester}}
\]

### (g)

\[
\boxed{\text{Phase-sequence meter}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 70 — Wrong Instrument Scenario
questions.question:
A student attempts to test insulation resistance using the resistance range of an ordinary multimeter.

**Why is this not equivalent to a proper insulation-resistance test? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
A normal multimeter resistance function uses a low internal test voltage.

An insulation-resistance tester applies a specified higher DC test voltage such as:

\[
250V,\quad500V,\quad1000V
\]

depending on the circuit and standard.

The higher test voltage stresses the insulation appropriately and detects leakage/breakdown that a low-voltage multimeter test may not reveal.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{ordinary resistance testing is not the same as insulation-resistance verification}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 71 — Full Load-Assessment Problem
questions.answer:
### (a) Connected load

\[
4+10+6+8=28kW
\]

\[
\boxed{P_{\text{connected}}=28kW}
\]

### (b) Maximum demand

\[
3.6+6.0+3.0+4.8=17.4kW
\]

\[
\boxed{P_{MD}=17.4kW}
\]

### (c) Demand factor

\[
DF=\frac{17.4}{28}
\]

\[
DF=0.6214
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{DF\approx0.62}
\]

or about:

\[
\boxed{62\%}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 72 — Diversity-Factor Scenario
questions.question:
Four departments have individual maximum demands of:

\[
20,\quad25,\quad30,\quad15kW
\]

The maximum simultaneous demand of the building is:

\[
60kW
\]

Calculate diversity factor. **(5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Sum of individual maximum demands:

\[
20+25+30+15=90kW
\]

Then:

\[
\text{Diversity Factor}=\frac{90}{60}
\]

\[
\boxed{1.5}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 73 — Explain Diversity to an Examiner
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“What is diversity, why do we use it, and what is the danger of using too much diversity?”**

Give a complete answer. **(10 marks)**

questions.title: Question 74 — Explain Selectivity to an Examiner
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“What is discrimination or selectivity, and why does it matter?”**

Give a complete answer. **(10 marks)**

questions.title: Question 75 — Explain Electrical First Aid to an Examiner
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“A person has received an electric shock. Explain what you do.”**

Give a strong, safe answer. **(15 marks)**
questions.answer:
A strong answer is:

### 1. Protect Yourself First

Do not touch the casualty while they are still in contact with electricity.

Make the scene safe.

If possible:

- switch off;
- isolate;
- disconnect the supply safely.

### 2. Activate Help

Call or instruct someone to contact emergency medical services.

Obtain an AED if available.

### 3. Assess the Casualty

Once it is safe to approach:

- check responsiveness;
- check normal breathing;
- identify major life-threatening injury.

### 4. If Not Breathing Normally

Begin CPR according to current training.

Adult CPR commonly uses:

\[
\boxed{100-120\text{ compressions/min}}
\]

and, for a trained rescuer:

\[
\boxed{30:2}
\]

compression-to-breath cycles.

### 5. Use AED

Turn on the AED and follow its instructions.

Ensure nobody touches the casualty during rhythm analysis or shock delivery.

### 6. If Breathing

Maintain the airway.

Monitor the casualty continuously.

Use an appropriate recovery position where suitable and where trauma does not make movement unsafe.

### 7. Treat Burns/Injuries

Electrical burns can hide deeper injury.

Cool burns appropriately and arrange medical assessment.

Also consider:

- falls;
- fractures;
- head injury;
- spinal injury.

### 8. Continue Monitoring

The casualty can deteriorate even after appearing to recover.

The key sequence is:

\[
\boxed{\text{make safe}\rightarrow\text{call for help}\rightarrow\text{assess}\rightarrow\text{CPR/AED if required}\rightarrow\text{monitor}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 76 — Explain Measuring Instruments to an Examiner
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“Name the main instruments you use when testing an installation and tell me what each one proves.”**

Give a complete answer. **(15 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Two-Pole Voltage Detector

Used to:

- identify voltage;
- prove a circuit dead.

Used with a proving unit.

### Low-Resistance Continuity Tester

Used for:

- CPC continuity;
- bonding;
- \(R_1+R_2\);
- ring continuity.

### Insulation-Resistance Tester

Used to verify insulation between conductors at an appropriate DC test voltage.

### Earth-Fault Loop Impedance Tester

Used to determine:

- \(Z_e\);
- \(Z_s\)

where live measurement is necessary.

### RCD Tester

Used to verify:

- RCD operation;
- trip time/current response according to the applicable test method.

### Clamp Meter

Used to measure current without opening the conductor.

Can assist with:

- load measurement;
- phase balancing;
- leakage-current investigation.

### Phase-Sequence Meter

Used to confirm phase order in a three-phase system.

### Earth-Electrode Tester

Used to determine earth-electrode resistance using a suitable method.

### Multimeter

Useful for:

- voltage;
- resistance;
- current;
- frequency;
- basic diagnostics.

However, a multimeter does not replace specialized installation-test instruments where a specified test method is required.

---

title: Kenya & EPRA regulations
sourceTitle: Step 8 — Kenya / EPRA Regulatory Framework, Licensing, Installation Responsibilities, Certification, Standards and Legal Compliance — Strengthened Distinction Edition

questions.title: Question 1 — What Is EPRA?
questions.question: **What is EPRA and what is its role in the electricity subsector? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 2 — Principal Statute
questions.question: **What is the principal Act currently governing electrical installation work in Kenya? (2 marks)**
questions.answer:
The principal statute is:

\[
\boxed{\text{The Energy Act, 2019}}
\]

The electrical-installation provisions relevant to workers and contractors are principally found in sections:

\[
\boxed{148\text{ to }152}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 3 — Why National Regulations Matter
questions.question: **Why is technical skill alone not enough for an electrical worker? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 4 — Act, Regulations and Standards
questions.question: **Differentiate between an Act of Parliament, regulations/rules and a technical standard. (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
A distinction answer should identify the **hierarchy and authority** of each source.

### Act of Parliament

An Act is primary legislation passed through the national legislative process.

Example:

\[
\boxed{\text{Energy Act, 2019}}
\]

It establishes broad legal duties, powers, offences and regulatory authority.

### Regulations or Rules

Regulations/rules are subsidiary legislation made under powers granted by an Act.

They provide more detailed operational requirements.

Example:

\[
\boxed{\text{Electric Power (Electrical Installation Work) Rules, 2006}}
\]

### Technical Standard

A standard provides technical requirements, specifications or methods.

Example:

\[
\boxed{\text{KS 662 series}}
\]

A standard is not the same thing as an Act, though legislation, contracts or regulatory requirements may require compliance with it.

---

questions.title: Question 5 — Energy Act Section 148
questions.topic: Authorization to Carry Out Electrical Installation Work
questions.question: **What is the main requirement of section 148 of the Energy Act, 2019 regarding electrical installation work? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Section 148 requires a person who wishes to carry out electrical installation work to do so through the licensing framework administered by the Authority.

A person carrying out installation work as an electrical contractor must be licensed by EPRA.

To qualify as an electrical contractor, the person must either:

- be a certified electrical worker;
- or employ a certified electrical worker.

The main principle is:

\[
\boxed{\text{electrical installation work is a regulated activity}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 6 — Certified Worker vs Licensed Contractor
questions.topic: Authorization to Carry Out Electrical Installation Work
questions.question: **Differentiate between a certified electrical worker and a licensed electrical contractor. (6 marks)**
questions.answer:
### Electrical Worker

An electrical worker is the technically certified person authorized to carry out the class of electrical work specified in the worker's certificate.

### Electrical Contractor

An electrical contractor is the person/business licensed to undertake electrical installation work as a contractor.

Under the Energy Act, a contractor must:

- be a certified electrical worker;
- or employ a certified electrical worker.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{worker certification and contractor licensing are related but not identical}}
\]

A worker certificate demonstrates the individual's authorized technical class.

A contractor licence authorizes the contracting business activity.

---

questions.title: Question 7 — Why the Distinction Matters
questions.topic: Authorization to Carry Out Electrical Installation Work
questions.question: **Why is it incorrect to assume that holding an electrical-worker certificate automatically gives unlimited authority to undertake any electrical contracting work? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
There are two separate issues:

1. **technical class/scope** of the worker;
2. **contractor authorization** for undertaking electrical installation work as a business/contractor.

The work must also remain within the class of work for which the person is authorized.

Therefore:

- holding a worker certificate does not remove contractor-licensing requirements;
- holding a licence does not allow work beyond the technical class/scope.

---

questions.title: Question 8 — Working Outside Licence Scope
questions.topic: Authorization to Carry Out Electrical Installation Work
questions.question:
A worker is competent in practice but undertakes installation work outside the class authorized by the worker's certificate.

**Why is this unacceptable? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 9 — Current C2 Installation Scope
questions.question: **According to EPRA's current assessment competency document, what installation scope is associated with C2 competency? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 10 — C2 Technical Areas
questions.question: **State ten technical areas included in the current EPRA C2 competency scope. (10 marks)**

questions.title: Question 11 — C2 Building Scenario
questions.question:
A three-storey residential building requires a complete new installation.

**Would this fall within the building-height scope stated in the current C2 competency document? Explain. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

The current C2 competency document states:

\[
\boxed{\text{up to two storeys}}
\]

A three-storey building exceeds that stated C2 scope.

The work would therefore require the appropriate higher authorization/class and must not be undertaken merely because it is residential.

---

questions.title: Question 12 — C2 Three-Phase Scenario
questions.question:
A two-storey building has a three-phase incoming supply.

**Is three-phase installation work part of the current C2 competency scope? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

The current C2 competency scope is based on:

\[
\boxed{\text{low-voltage single-phase systems}}
\]

Three-phase installation work is part of the additional C1 competency level.

---

questions.title: Question 13 — Current C1 Installation Scope
questions.question: **According to the current EPRA competency document, what additional installation scope is associated with C1? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 14 — Additional C1 Competencies
questions.question: **State six major areas added at C1 beyond the C2 foundation. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 15 — C1 Building Scenario
questions.question:
A four-storey low-voltage commercial building, not a factory or public-entertainment premises, requires a three-phase electrical installation.

**Does the current C1 competency document include this type of work within its stated assessment scope? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 16 — Five-Storey Scenario
questions.question:
A five-storey building requires a three-phase installation.

**Why should a C1 candidate not assume that C1 authorization is sufficient? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The current C1 assessment scope states:

\[
\boxed{\text{up to four storeys}}
\]

A five-storey building falls outside that stated scope.

The electrician must confirm the class of authorization legally required before undertaking the work.

---

questions.title: Question 17 — Energy Act Section 149
questions.question: **What is the purpose of section 149 of the Energy Act, 2019? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 18 — Why EPRA Tests Candidates
questions.question: **Why does EPRA use written and oral competency assessment? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 19 — Certificate Conditions
questions.question: **Why must an electrical worker pay attention to any conditions attached to a certificate? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
A certificate may authorize only particular classes or conditions of electrical work.

The holder must comply with those restrictions.

Ignoring conditions can amount to:

- unauthorized work;
- regulatory breach;
- unsafe practice.

The certificate is therefore not merely proof of training; it defines the worker's legal authorization.

---

questions.title: Question 20 — Section 151 Owner/Occupier Duty
questions.topic: Duties of the Owner or Occupier
questions.question: **What duty does section 151 of the Energy Act place on the owner or occupier of premises regarding electrical installation work? (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 21 — Owner Hires Unlicensed Person
questions.topic: Duties of the Owner or Occupier
questions.question:
A homeowner knowingly hires an unauthorized person to carry out electrical installation work because the price is cheaper.

**Why is the homeowner also at fault? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
The Energy Act does not place responsibility only on the person physically carrying out the work.

The owner/occupier has a duty to ensure that installation work is carried out by an authorized electrical contractor.

Therefore knowingly permitting unauthorized installation work can itself constitute an offence.

---

questions.title: Question 22 — Periodic Inspection
questions.topic: Duties of the Owner or Occupier
questions.question: **Why does the Energy Act require electrical installations to be periodically inspected and defects remedied? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 23 — Certification Before Initial Connection
questions.question: **Why must installation certification be completed before initial connection to the electricity supply? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 24 — Utility Refuses Connection
questions.question:
An electrical installation fails safety inspection.

**Can the connection provider be required to energize it simply because the owner has paid for connection? Explain. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

Under the Energy Act, supply may be refused where the electrical installation does not satisfy the required conditions.

Safety takes precedence over the owner's desire for immediate connection.

Defects must be corrected before the premises is accepted for safe supply.

---

questions.title: Question 25 — Discontinuation of Existing Supply
questions.question: **Can an existing electrical supply be discontinued where an installation is found to be unsafe? Explain. (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 26 — Purpose of a Completion Certificate
questions.question: **What is the purpose of an electrical installation completion certificate? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 27 — Why Test Results Matter
questions.question: **Why should a completion certificate be supported by actual electrical test results? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 28 — False Certification
questions.question: **Why is knowingly submitting false electrical certification a serious matter? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 29 — As-Built Information
questions.question: **Why are accurate circuit schedules and as-built information valuable after an installation is completed? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 30 — Section 152
questions.question: **What is the general purpose of section 152 of the Energy Act, 2019? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
Section 152 creates offences and penalties relating to unauthorized electrical installation work.

It addresses:

- unauthorized persons carrying out electrical installation work;
- consumers permitting unauthorized work;
- entities permitting unauthorized persons to undertake electrical work.

The purpose is to discourage unsafe and unregulated installation activity.

---

questions.title: Question 31 — Unauthorized Worker Penalty
questions.question: Under section 152, what penalty may apply to a person carrying out electrical installation work without being duly authorized? **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The Act provides for a penalty on conviction of up to:

\[
\boxed{KSh\,100,000}
\]

or imprisonment for up to:

\[
\boxed{6\text{ months}}
\]

or both.

The important principle is that unauthorized installation work is an offence, not merely poor professional practice.

---

questions.title: Question 32 — Consumer Allowing Unauthorized Work
questions.question: What penalty may apply to a consumer who permits unauthorized electrical installation work in the premises? **(4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The Act provides for a penalty on conviction of up to:

\[
\boxed{KSh\,50,000}
\]

or imprisonment for up to:

\[
\boxed{3\text{ months}}
\]

or both.

This reinforces the owner's legal duty to use duly authorized persons.

---

questions.title: Question 33 — Why Penalties Apply to Consumers Too
questions.question: **Why does the law penalize a consumer who knowingly allows unauthorized electrical work? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 34 — Current EPRA Listing
questions.question: **Which older electrical-installation rules are still listed by EPRA among its electricity regulatory instruments? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
EPRA currently lists:

\[
\boxed{\text{Electric Power (Electrical Installation Work) Rules, 2006}}
\]

These rules were originally made under the earlier electricity legislation but remain important in the present administrative framework while replacement regulations are still being developed.

---

questions.title: Question 35 — Application of the 2006 Rules
questions.question: **What geographical application did the 2006 Rules state? (2 marks)**
questions.answer:
The Rules state that they apply to:

\[
\boxed{\text{all premises and areas in Kenya}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 36 — Definition of Electrical Installation
questions.question: Under the 2006 Rules, what broad items are included within an electrical installation? **(5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 37 — Electrical Installation Work
questions.question: **What types of activities are generally considered electrical installation work? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 38 — Draft vs Enacted Regulation
questions.question: **Why must a student distinguish between a draft regulation and an enacted regulation? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 39 — Current EPRA Draft Position
questions.question: **What is the safe exam approach to the newer Energy (Electricity Supply and Installation Work) draft regulations? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 40 — Why Draft Licence Classes Can Mislead
questions.question: **Why is it dangerous to memorize licence-class names from consultation drafts instead of the current EPRA competency document? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
Draft regulations have proposed revised class structures at different stages.

Those proposed structures do not necessarily match the current C2/C1 examination classes.

Therefore using draft class labels could cause the student to:

- reverse C1/C2 scopes;
- quote future proposals as current law;
- give the wrong exam answer.

For this study bank, the current official EPRA competency sheet is used for C2/C1 assessment scope.

---

questions.title: Question 41 — What Is KS 662?
questions.question: **What is the KS 662 series? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 42 — Current Published KEBS Editions
questions.question: **Which KS 662 parts are clearly listed by KEBS as 2018 editions in its current webstore? (4 marks)**

questions.title: Question 43 — 2026 Draft Revision
questions.question: **What is important about the 2026 KS 662 draft revision currently published by KEBS? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
KEBS published draft revisions in 2026 for public review.

The draft KS 662-1:2026 states that it is intended as a third edition replacing the 2018 second edition once finalized.

It is based on:

- BS 7671:2018 and its amendments;
- IEC 60364 series.

However:

\[
\boxed{\text{a draft Kenya Standard should not be treated as the final published standard until formally issued}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 44 — Relationship Between KS 662 and BS 7671
questions.question: **Why are many BS 7671 concepts useful for a Kenyan electrician even though Kenya has its own standards? (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 45 — Why Edition Checking Matters
questions.question: **Why must a technician check the edition/date of a standard rather than simply remembering a table value from training? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 46 — Why Approved/Compliant Materials Matter
questions.question: **Why should electrical materials and equipment conform to applicable standards? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 47 — Correct Rating
questions.question: **Why is it unlawful/unsafe in principle to install a conductor or apparatus that is undersized for its intended duty? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 48 — Who Is Responsible for Testing?
questions.question: **Why must the licensed person responsible for installation work ensure it is properly tested rather than leaving testing entirely to the utility? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 49 — Utility Inspection Does Not Transfer Responsibility
questions.question:
A connection provider inspects an installation before connection.

**Does this remove responsibility from the electrical contractor for defective workmanship? Explain. (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

The contractor remains responsible for the work performed and certified.

The utility's connection inspection is an additional control.

It does not convert poor workmanship into compliant work.

---

questions.title: Question 50 — Defect Found After Certification
questions.question:
A defect is discovered after a completion certificate has been issued.

**What should a competent contractor do? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 51 — Signing Work You Did Not Verify
questions.question:
A licensed worker is asked to sign a completion certificate for work done by someone else without inspecting or testing it.

**Should the worker sign? Explain. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 52 — Client Requests Unsafe Shortcut
questions.question:
A client asks the electrician to omit earthing because “the house is only temporary.”

**How should the electrician respond? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 53 — Client Wants Oversized Breaker
questions.question:
A client complains that an MCB trips and asks for a larger breaker.

**What regulatory/professional principle applies? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 54 — Unauthorized Alteration
questions.question:
A homeowner has a licensed installation but later pays an unlicensed person to add three socket-outlets.

**Is the original installation certificate enough to make the new work acceptable? Explain. (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 55 — C2 Worker Asked for Three-Phase Work
questions.question:
A C2 worker is asked to install a three-phase distribution board in a commercial building.

**What should the worker do? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
The current C2 competency scope is single-phase.

The worker should not undertake the three-phase work merely because the technical task appears familiar.

The work should be handled under the appropriate higher authorization, such as the applicable C1 level or other required class.

---

questions.title: Question 56 — C1 Worker Asked to Wire Factory
questions.question:
A C1 worker is asked to carry out a new installation in a factory.

**Why must the worker not rely only on the fact that the system is low-voltage three-phase? (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
The current C1 competency scope specifically excludes factories and places designated for public entertainment.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{voltage and phase alone do not define licence scope}}
\]

Building use and other class restrictions also matter.

The worker must confirm the appropriate authorization before starting.

---

questions.title: Question 57 — Four-Storey Residential Three-Phase Building
questions.question:
A four-storey residential building is supplied at low-voltage three-phase.

It is not a factory or public-entertainment premises.

**Which current EPRA assessment class contains this technical scope? (4 marks)**
questions.answer:
The current EPRA competency document places this within:

\[
\boxed{\text{C1}}
\]

because C1 includes low-voltage three-phase installation work in buildings up to four storeys, subject to the stated exclusions.

---

questions.title: Question 58 — Two-Storey Single-Phase House
questions.question:
A two-storey house requires a new low-voltage single-phase installation.

**Which current EPRA competency class directly covers this technical scope? (3 marks)**
questions.answer:
The stated scope corresponds to:

\[
\boxed{\text{C2}}
\]

subject to all other licensing and contractor requirements.

---

questions.title: Question 59 — Why C1 Includes C2 Knowledge
questions.question: **Why does the current C1 competency document state that C1 includes the C2 competency areas? (5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 60 — Technical Standard vs Licence Scope
questions.question:
A technician knows how to design a three-phase circuit correctly according to a technical standard.

**Does technical design competence alone authorize the technician to install it? Explain. (5 marks)**
questions.answer:
No.

Two separate requirements exist:

### Technical compliance

The design must comply with applicable standards.

### Legal authorization

The worker/contractor must hold the appropriate authorization for the class of work.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{correct design does not replace licensing}}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{\text{licensing does not replace correct design}}
\]

Both are required.

---

questions.title: Question 61 — Why National Standards Must Be Mentioned
questions.question: **If an EPRA oral examiner asks what governs electrical installation work in Kenya, why is answering only “BS 7671” incomplete? (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 62 — Explain the Kenyan Regulatory Framework
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“What governs electrical installation work in Kenya?”**

Give a strong answer. **(12 marks)**
questions.answer:
A strong answer is:

Electrical installation work in Kenya is governed by a combination of:

### 1. Primary Legislation

The:

\[
\boxed{\text{Energy Act, 2019}}
\]

provides the main legal framework.

Sections 148–152 address:

- authorization;
- electrical workers;
- contractors;
- installation duties;
- unauthorized work.

### 2. EPRA Regulation and Licensing

EPRA:

- certifies electrical workers;
- licenses contractors;
- enforces compliance;
- defines assessment competency areas;
- monitors safety and technical requirements.

### 3. Subsidiary Rules/Regulations

EPRA currently lists the:

\[
\boxed{\text{Electric Power (Electrical Installation Work) Rules, 2006}}
\]

among the applicable electricity regulatory instruments while replacement regulations remain under development.

### 4. Kenya Standards

Electrical installation work must follow applicable national technical standards, including the:

\[
\boxed{\text{KS 662 series}}
\]

and other relevant equipment standards.

### 5. Licensing Scope

The worker must stay within the class authorized by EPRA.

Technical knowledge alone does not authorize work outside that scope.

---

questions.title: Question 63 — Explain C2 vs C1
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“What is the main technical difference between C2 and C1?”**

Give a complete answer. **(10 marks)**

questions.title: Question 64 — Explain Worker vs Contractor
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“What is the difference between an electrical worker and an electrical contractor?”**

Give a complete answer. **(8 marks)**
questions.answer:
An electrical worker is the individual whose competence is certified by EPRA for a particular class of work.

An electrical contractor is the person/business licensed to undertake electrical installation work as a contracting activity.

A contractor must be:

- a certified electrical worker;
- or employ a certified electrical worker.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{worker = technical person}}
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{contractor = licensed contracting entity/person}}
\]

Both the individual technical scope and contractor authorization must be correct for the job.

---

questions.title: Question 65 — Explain Owner Responsibilities
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“What responsibility does the premises owner have?”**

Give a strong answer. **(8 marks)**

questions.title: Question 66 — Draft Regulation Quoted as Law
questions.question:
A candidate says:

> “The 2024 draft electrical-installation regulations changed all current licence classes, so the old current C1/C2 scope no longer applies.”

What is wrong with the answer? **(6 marks)**
questions.answer:
A consultation draft is not automatically enacted law.

The candidate must verify whether a final legal instrument has actually come into force.

EPRA's current competency document still uses the existing C2/C1 assessment structure.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{do not replace current official requirements with unfinalized draft proposals}}
\]

---

questions.title: Question 67 — Current EPRA Site Evidence
questions.question: **What is the safest current source hierarchy when revising licensing/regulatory facts for an EPRA exam? (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 68 — BS 7671 Value vs Kenya Exam
questions.question:
A training video says a particular design value comes from a BS 7671 table.

**How should a Kenyan EPRA candidate use that information? (6 marks)**

questions.title: Question 69 — Outdated Standard
questions.question:
A contractor has an old copy of a Kenya wiring standard and says:

> “It was legal when I bought it, so I never need a newer edition.”

Why is this poor professional practice? **(5 marks)**

questions.title: Question 70 — Full Compliance Scenario
questions.question:
A client asks a C2 electrical worker to install a new single-phase system in a two-storey house.

Describe the regulatory and technical steps that should be considered before the installation is energized. **(15 marks)**

questions.title: Question 71 — Full C1 Compliance Scenario
questions.question:
A C1 worker is responsible for a four-storey, low-voltage three-phase commercial installation.

State ten additional matters that require particular attention compared with a simple C2 domestic installation. **(10 marks)**

questions.title: Question 72 — Complete EPRA Regulatory Answer
questions.question:
An examiner asks:

> **“You have passed the electrical calculations. Why should EPRA license you, and what legal responsibilities will you carry once licensed?”**

Give a strong professional answer. **(15 marks)**

title: C1 full mock exam
sourceTitle: FULL MOCK WRITTEN INTERVIEW — DISTINCTION EDITION
notes:
# EPRA ELECTRICAL WORKER LICENCE CLASS C1
## FULL MOCK WRITTEN INTERVIEW — DISTINCTION EDITION

**TIME: 2 HOURS**  
**TOTAL MARKS: 100**

> **Important:** This is an original practice examination constructed to closely reproduce the structure, density, mark allocation and question style seen in freely accessible EPRA/ERC C1 written papers, especially the 2025 papers, while using the current EPRA competency scope.
>
> It is **not an official EPRA paper** and contains no leaked questions.

---

# INSTRUCTIONS

A. Fill in your candidate details as required.

B. Make sure this paper is for **Electrical Worker Licence Class C1**.

C. **Answer ALL questions.**

D. Show all working in calculation questions. Unsupported numerical answers may lose method marks.

E. Where a question asks for a definition, give a precise technical definition before adding explanation.

F. Unless otherwise stated, use the numerical data supplied in the question.

| Question No. | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Maximum Marks | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 |
| Marks Obtained |  |  |  |  |  |

---

# END OF EXAM PAPER

---

# DISTINCTION-LEVEL MARKING SCHEME AND FULL TEACHING ANSWERS

> **How to use this answer section**
>
> Do the complete paper first under the 2-hour limit. Then mark it using this section.
>
> For calculations, the expected method is:
>
> \[
> \boxed{\text{GIVEN}\rightarrow\text{FORMULA}\rightarrow\text{SUBSTITUTE}\rightarrow\text{ANSWER}\rightarrow\text{CHECK}}
> \]
>
> For explanation questions, a distinction answer should normally show:
>
> \[
> \boxed{\text{What it is}\rightarrow\text{Why it matters}\rightarrow\text{How it works}\rightarrow\text{What happens if wrong}}
> \]
>
> Where a formal BS 7671 term is used, the precise definition wording is based on the uploaded official BS 7671 Seventeenth Edition Part 2 Definitions, as previously requested. The older book is used for wording of definitions, not as authority for current 2026 numerical requirements.

---

# C1 DISTINCTION ANSWER STANDARD

A distinction-level candidate should consistently demonstrate all of the following:

## Definitions

Give the precise definition first, then explain it in plain technical language.

## Calculations

Always show:

\[
\boxed{
\text{known quantities}
\rightarrow
\text{formula}
\rightarrow
\text{substitution}
\rightarrow
\text{answer with unit}
\rightarrow
\text{sense check}
}
\]

## Motors

Do not memorize star/delta labels alone. Relate them to:

\[
V_L,\quad V_{ph},\quad I_L,\quad I_{ph}
\]

and the nameplate.

## Power Factor

Explain that poor PF causes higher current for the same kW, and that capacitors correct reactive power rather than “reducing the motor's real power.”

## Earthing and Testing

Always connect a test to its safety purpose:

- continuity → protective path exists;
- IR → insulation separates conductors;
- loop impedance → enough fault current for disconnection;
- electrode test → effectiveness of Earth connection.

## Safe Working

Never write only “switch off.”

A complete isolation answer includes:

- identify;
- isolate;
- secure;
- prove dead;
- re-prove tester.

---

**End of Expanded C1 Marking Scheme and Full Teaching Answers**

questions.title: QUESTION 1 — MULTIPLE CHOICE (20 MARKS)
questions.question:
For Questions 1–20, choose the **ONE BEST answer**. Each question carries **1 mark**.

### 1.
Which installation is within the **current published C1 competency scope**, assuming no other special restriction applies?

A. A six-storey residential building  
B. A four-storey ordinary office building supplied at low-voltage three-phase  
C. A small tea-processing factory  
D. A two-storey nightclub

### 2.
The instrument that measures electrical energy consumed over time is a:

A. Wattmeter  
B. Energy meter  
C. Ammeter  
D. Insulation-resistance tester

### 3.
In a balanced three-phase star-connected load, the neutral current is ideally:

A. Equal to line current  
B. \(\sqrt3\) times line current  
C. Zero  
D. Three times phase current

### 4.
For a balanced delta-connected load:

A. \(V_L=\sqrt3V_{ph}\)  
B. \(V_L=V_{ph}\)  
C. \(I_L=I_{ph}\)  
D. \(V_{ph}=V_L/\sqrt3\)

### 5.
Improving the power factor of an inductive load, while its real power remains unchanged, normally:

A. Increases supply current  
B. Reduces supply current  
C. Increases real power automatically  
D. Makes frequency increase

### 6.
The synchronous speed of a six-pole machine supplied at 50 Hz is:

A. 500 rpm  
B. 750 rpm  
C. 1000 rpm  
D. 1500 rpm

### 7.
The normal method of reversing the direction of rotation of a three-phase induction motor is to:

A. Reverse neutral and earth  
B. Interchange any two line conductors  
C. Reduce the supply voltage  
D. Increase the number of poles

### 8.
Which part of a Class I motor should be connected to protective earth?

A. Rotor winding  
B. Stator winding  
C. Metallic enclosure  
D. Winding insulation

### 9.
Which instrument is specifically intended to verify three-phase phase order?

A. Clamp meter  
B. Phase-sequence indicator  
C. Insulation tester  
D. Earth-electrode tester

### 10.
An RCD principally responds to:

A. Excessive line current only  
B. A residual-current imbalance between live conductors  
C. Low supply frequency  
D. Excessive power factor

### 11.
For a circuit requiring overload protection, the basic cable/protective-device relationship is:

A. \(I_Z \le I_B \le I_N\)  
B. \(I_N \le I_Z \le I_B\)  
C. \(I_B \le I_N \le I_Z\)  
D. \(I_B=I_Z<I_N\)

### 12.
The primary function of a motor thermal overload relay is to protect against:

A. Sustained motor overload  
B. Lightning surges  
C. Low insulation resistance during dead testing  
D. Reverse phase sequence only

### 13.
If earth-fault loop impedance \(Z_s\) decreases while supply voltage remains unchanged, earth-fault current will generally:

A. Decrease  
B. Increase  
C. Remain unchanged  
D. Become zero

### 14.
A 4-pole induction motor supplied at 50 Hz has a synchronous speed of:

A. 750 rpm  
B. 1000 rpm  
C. 1500 rpm  
D. 3000 rpm

### 15.
A motor nameplate marked **400/690 V Δ/Y** should normally be connected on a 400 V supply in:

A. Star  
B. Delta  
C. Open delta  
D. Series

### 16.
During star-delta starting, the line starting current in star is approximately what fraction of the delta/DOL line starting current, under the usual simplified comparison?

A. One-half  
B. One-third  
C. \(\sqrt3\) times  
D. Three times

### 17.
Which load is most characteristically associated with a lagging power factor?

A. Pure resistance heater  
B. Incandescent filament treated as resistive  
C. Induction motor  
D. Capacitor bank

### 18.
The synchronous speed formula is:

A. \(N_s=120P/f\)  
B. \(N_s=fP/120\)  
C. \(N_s=120f/P\)  
D. \(N_s=P/(120f)\)

### 19.
A 400 V star-connected winding has an approximate phase voltage of:

A. 133 V  
B. 230 V  
C. 400 V  
D. 690 V

### 20.
After correcting the power factor of an unchanged motor load, which quantity remains approximately unchanged?

A. Real power required by the load  
B. Supply current  
C. Reactive power drawn from the supply  
D. Apparent power

---
questions.answer:
# QUESTION 1 — FULL ANSWERS AND EXPLANATIONS

Each item carries **1 mark**, but the explanation below teaches the concept at the depth needed for oral follow-up questions.

## 1. Correct answer: **B**

A four-storey ordinary office building supplied at low-voltage three-phase falls within the present published C1 technical assessment scope, subject to any other applicable restriction.

The essential C1 scope points are:

- low-voltage;
- three-phase;
- buildings up to four storeys;
- excludes factories;
- excludes places designated for public entertainment.

### Why the other choices fail

- **A — six storeys:** exceeds the stated four-storey C1 scope.
- **C — factory:** factories are excluded from the stated C1 scope.
- **D — nightclub:** a nightclub is a place of public entertainment and falls within the stated exclusion.

### Exam habit

When licence-scope questions appear, do not answer from voltage alone. Check:

\[
\boxed{\text{phase system + building height + building use + exclusions}}
\]

---

## 2. Correct answer: **B — Energy meter**

An energy meter measures electrical energy used over time, commonly in:

\[
\boxed{kWh}
\]

A wattmeter measures instantaneous real power in watts.

The relationship is:

\[
E=Pt
\]

Therefore an energy meter effectively accumulates power use over time.

---

## 3. Correct answer: **C — Zero**

In a perfectly balanced three-phase star system:

- the three phase currents have equal magnitude;
- they are displaced by \(120^\circ\);
- their vector sum is zero.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{I_N=0}
\]

in the ideal balanced case.

### Important distinction

This does **not** mean neutral is always zero in a real installation. Neutral current can arise from:

- unequal single-phase loading;
- harmonics;
- faults;
- poor connections.

---

## 4. Correct answer: **B — \(V_L=V_{ph}\)**

For a balanced delta connection:

\[
\boxed{V_L=V_{ph}}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{I_L=\sqrt3\,I_{ph}}
\]

Why? Each winding is connected directly between two line conductors, so each winding receives the full line-to-line voltage.

---

## 5. Correct answer: **B — Reduces supply current**

For a balanced three-phase load:

\[
P=\sqrt3V_LI_L\cos\phi
\]

Rearrange:

\[
I_L=\frac{P}{\sqrt3V_L\cos\phi}
\]

If:

- real power \(P\) stays the same;
- voltage stays the same;
- power factor increases;

then the denominator increases and current falls.

This reduces:

- cable heating;
- voltage drop;
- kVA demand;
- transformer loading.

---

## 6. Correct answer: **C — 1000 rpm**

Use:

\[
N_s=\frac{120f}{P}
\]

Given:

\[
f=50Hz,\qquad P=6
\]

Substitute:

\[
N_s=\frac{120\times50}{6}
\]

\[
N_s=\frac{6000}{6}
\]

\[
\boxed{N_s=1000rpm}
\]

### Check

More poles produce lower synchronous speed. A six-pole motor must run slower than a four-pole 50 Hz motor at 1500 rpm, so 1000 rpm is reasonable.

---

## 7. Correct answer: **B — Interchange any two line conductors**

Changing any two phases reverses the phase sequence.

For example:

\[
L1-L2-L3
\]

becomes:

\[
L1-L3-L2
\]

The rotating magnetic field reverses, so a normal three-phase induction motor reverses rotation.

---

## 8. Correct answer: **C — Metallic enclosure**

The exposed metal enclosure of Class I equipment is connected to the protective conductor.

If insulation fails and line touches the enclosure:

1. enclosure becomes live;
2. fault current flows through the CPC;
3. protective device should disconnect;
4. duration of dangerous touch voltage is limited.

The winding itself is not “earthed” as the normal protective measure.

---

## 9. Correct answer: **B — Phase-sequence indicator**

A phase-sequence indicator identifies the order of the three phase voltages.

It is used when phase order matters, especially for:

- motors;
- pumps;
- fans;
- compressors;
- phase-sensitive equipment.

---

## 10. Correct answer: **B — Residual-current imbalance**

In a healthy single-phase circuit:

\[
I_L\approx I_N
\]

If some current leaks to Earth:

\[
I_L\neq I_N
\]

The RCD detects the residual difference:

\[
I_\Delta=|I_L-I_N|
\]

and disconnects when the operating conditions are met.

### Key distinction

An RCD is not automatically an overload-protection device.

---

## 11. Correct answer: **C — \(I_B\leq I_N\leq I_Z\)**

Where overload protection is required:

\[
\boxed{I_B\leq I_N\leq I_Z}
\]

where:

- \(I_B\) = circuit design current;
- \(I_N\) = rated current of protective device;
- \(I_Z\) = current-carrying capacity of the cable under installed conditions.

### Meaning

- If \(I_N<I_B\), the protective device may trip in normal service.
- If \(I_N>I_Z\), the cable may overload before the protective device disconnects.

---

## 12. Correct answer: **A — Sustained motor overload**

A thermal overload relay is intended to protect a motor from excessive thermal stress caused by sustained overcurrent.

Possible causes include:

- excessive mechanical load;
- locked/stalled condition;
- single phasing;
- prolonged starting.

It is not a substitute for a short-circuit protective device.

---

## 13. Correct answer: **B — Increase**

Approximate fault current is:

\[
I_f=\frac{U_0}{Z_s}
\]

Therefore if \(Z_s\) decreases:

\[
I_f\uparrow
\]

A larger earth-fault current generally causes an overcurrent device to operate more quickly.

---

## 14. Correct answer: **C — 1500 rpm**

\[
N_s=\frac{120\times50}{4}
\]

\[
N_s=\frac{6000}{4}
\]

\[
\boxed{1500rpm}
\]

A practical induction motor with four poles would normally run slightly below this speed because of slip.

---

## 15. Correct answer: **B — Delta**

A nameplate marked:

\[
400/690V\quad\Delta/Y
\]

means the winding is designed for about 400 V.

At 400 V line voltage:

\[
\boxed{\Delta}
\]

because:

\[
V_{ph}=V_L=400V
\]

At 690 V line voltage, star gives:

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{690}{\sqrt3}\approx398V
\]

---

## 16. Correct answer: **B — One-third**

During star starting, each winding receives:

\[
\frac{V_L}{\sqrt3}
\]

instead of full line voltage in delta.

Under the usual simplified comparison, star line starting current is about:

\[
\boxed{\frac13}
\]

of the delta/DOL starting line current.

---

## 17. Correct answer: **C — Induction motor**

An induction motor needs magnetizing current to create magnetic flux.

That current is inductive and lags voltage.

Therefore the motor normally has:

\[
\boxed{\text{lagging power factor}}
\]

---

## 18. Correct answer: **C — \(N_s=120f/P\)**

Remember:

\[
\boxed{N_s=\frac{120f}{P}}
\]

A good check is dimensional reasoning:

- frequency increases → speed increases;
- number of poles increases → speed decreases.

---

## 19. Correct answer: **B — approximately 230 V**

For star:

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{V_L}{\sqrt3}
\]

\[
V_{ph}=\frac{400}{1.732}
\]

\[
\boxed{V_{ph}\approx231V}
\]

---

## 20. Correct answer: **A — Real power required by the load**

Power-factor correction mainly reduces:

- reactive power drawn from the supply;
- apparent power;
- line current.

The real mechanical/electrical load remains approximately the same.

\[
\boxed{kW\approx\text{unchanged}}
\]

---

questions.title: QUESTION 2 — C1 SCOPE, SAFETY AND THREE-PHASE PRACTICE (20 MARKS)
questions.topic: C1 SCOPE, SAFETY AND THREE-PHASE PRACTICE
questions.question:
### (a)
State the **current published EPRA C1 technical scope** in relation to supply type, building height and principal exclusions. **(3 marks)**

### (b)
Giving a reason in each case, state whether a C1 worker should regard the following as falling within the current C1 assessment scope:

i. A small tea-processing factory supplied at 415 V.  
ii. A four-storey ordinary residential apartment supplied at low-voltage three-phase.  
iii. A two-storey nightclub supplied at 415 V. **(3 marks)**

### (c)
You are carrying out maintenance on one section of a three-phase building while other sections must remain energized. State **four precautions** that should be taken to prevent inadvertent energization of the section being worked on. **(4 marks)**

### (d)
State **two factors** to consider when selecting an electrical enclosure. **(2 marks)**

### (e)
State a common notation for:

i. Positive phase sequence.  
ii. Negative phase sequence. **(2 marks)**

### (f)
i. What can happen to a three-phase motor if any two phases are interchanged?  
ii. Name the instrument used to verify phase sequence. **(2 marks)**

### (g)
State **four factors** that should be considered when determining the interval between periodic inspection and testing of an electrical installation. **(4 marks)**

---
questions.answer:
# QUESTION 2 — FULL MODEL ANSWER

## (a) Current Published C1 Scope — 3 marks

A full-mark answer should contain all three ideas:

> C1 includes the C2 competencies and covers **low-voltage three-phase electrical installations in buildings up to four storeys**, excluding **factories and places designated for public entertainment**.

### Examiner expectation

Do not write only “C1 is three-phase.” That is incomplete.

The examiner is testing whether you know the legal/technical boundary of the licence assessment.

---

## (b) Premises Classification — 3 marks

### i. Small tea-processing factory supplied at 415 V — **No**

Reason:

\[
\boxed{\text{factory is excluded}}
\]

The fact that the voltage is within low-voltage three-phase does not remove the premises-use restriction.

### ii. Four-storey ordinary residential apartment supplied at LV three-phase — **Yes, in principle**

It is:

- low-voltage;
- three-phase;
- not above four storeys;
- not described as a factory/public-entertainment premises.

### iii. Two-storey nightclub supplied at 415 V — **No**

A nightclub is a place of public entertainment.

### Distinction principle

Licence scope is determined by more than one condition:

\[
\boxed{\text{voltage + phase + height + use + exclusions}}
\]

---

## (c) Preventing Inadvertent Energization — 4 marks

A distinction answer might say:

1. **Identify the correct section and every possible source.**  
   This includes main supply, generators, UPS systems, PV, backfeeds and interconnections.

2. **Isolate the section using a suitable isolating device.**

3. **Apply a personal lock-off device.**  
   The isolation should not be capable of being casually restored by another person.

4. **Attach a warning tag/notice.**

5. **Retain control of the lock-off key.**

6. **Prove dead using an approved voltage indicator.**

7. **Re-prove the tester after the dead test.**

8. **Communicate the isolation to affected personnel.**

### Why this matters

A breaker being OFF is not proof that the equipment is dead.

Possible dangers include:

- wrong breaker;
- faulty labelling;
- alternative supply;
- borrowed neutral;
- another person re-closing the device.

---

## (d) Enclosure Selection — 2 marks

Any two, one mark each:

- water/dust exposure and required IP degree;
- mechanical impact risk;
- corrosion;
- indoor/outdoor use;
- temperature;
- fire performance;
- accessibility to live parts;
- heat dissipation;
- chemical exposure.

### Strong answer example

> I would consider the environmental exposure and the required IP rating, and also whether the enclosure has sufficient mechanical strength for the location.

---

## (e) Phase Sequence — 2 marks

A common notation is:

Positive:

\[
\boxed{L1-L2-L3}
\]

Negative:

\[
\boxed{L1-L3-L2}
\]

Equivalent R-Y-B notation may be accepted if correctly defined.

---

## (f) Interchanging Two Phases — 2 marks

### i.

Interchanging any two phases reverses the phase sequence.

A normal three-phase induction motor will therefore reverse its direction of rotation.

### ii.

Instrument:

\[
\boxed{\text{phase-sequence indicator}}
\]

---

## (g) Periodic Inspection Interval — 4 marks

Any four well-developed factors:

### 1. Type of installation/use

A heavily used workshop may deteriorate more rapidly than a lightly used office.

### 2. Environmental conditions

Moisture, heat, dust, chemicals and mechanical damage can accelerate deterioration.

### 3. Age and present condition

An older installation or one showing deterioration may justify shorter intervals.

### 4. Quality of maintenance

Well-maintained installations generally present lower risk than neglected installations.

### 5. Previous test results

A history of deteriorating insulation or repeated defects can justify earlier reinspection.

### 6. Change in use

A building converted from residential to commercial use may require reassessment.

### Examiner expectation

The interval is based on:

\[
\boxed{\text{risk and condition}}
\]

not simply “every X years” unless a specific rule/guidance is explicitly asked.

---

questions.title: QUESTION 3 — EARTHING, BONDING AND TESTING (20 MARKS)
questions.question:
### (a)
Define **equipotential bonding**. **(2 marks)**

### (b)
State **two safety purposes** of protective equipotential bonding. **(2 marks)**

### (c)
Define a **circuit protective conductor (CPC)**. **(2 marks)**

### (d)
Explain the following earthing arrangements:

i. TN-C-S.  
ii. TT. **(4 marks)**

### (e)
Define an **earth electrode**. **(2 marks)**

### (f)
State the purpose of:

i. An earth-electrode resistance test.  
ii. An earth-fault loop impedance test. **(4 marks)**

### (g)
What is meant by a **floating/open neutral**, and state **two dangers** it can create in a three-phase four-wire installation. State one appropriate corrective action. **(4 marks)**

---
questions.answer:
# QUESTION 3 — FULL MODEL ANSWER

## (a) Equipotential Bonding — 2 marks

Formal definition:

> **Equipotential bonding:** Electrical connection maintaining various exposed-conductive-parts and extraneous-conductive-parts at substantially the same potential.

### What this means physically

The purpose is not primarily to carry normal load current.

Bonding reduces the voltage difference a person could bridge between two simultaneously accessible conductive parts.

Example:

- metal water pipe;
- exposed metal enclosure of electrical equipment.

If both are maintained near the same potential during a fault, the dangerous touch-voltage difference is reduced.

---

## (b) Safety Purposes of Protective Equipotential Bonding — 2 marks

Any two:

1. reduce dangerous touch-voltage differences;
2. keep simultaneously accessible conductive parts at substantially the same potential;
3. support protection against electric shock;
4. support the effectiveness of the overall ADS/earthing arrangement.

### Distinction explanation

Earthing and bonding are related but not identical:

- **earthing** provides a path back toward the source/Earth reference;
- **bonding** reduces potential differences between conductive parts.

---

## (c) CPC — 2 marks

Formal definition:

> **Circuit protective conductor (cpc):** A protective conductor connecting exposed-conductive-parts of equipment to the main earthing terminal.

### Practical meaning

The CPC:

- normally carries no load current;
- provides the protective path during a line-to-metal fault;
- helps fault current reach a level that causes automatic disconnection.

A visible green/yellow conductor is not enough; continuity must be verified.

---

## (d) Earthing Systems — 4 marks

### i. TN-C-S

In a TN-C-S arrangement:

- the source neutral is earthed;
- neutral and protective functions are combined in a PEN conductor over part of the supply;
- they are separated into distinct neutral and protective conductors at/near the consumer installation.

During a fault, current returns principally through a metallic protective path.

### Safety significance

A broken/high-resistance PEN conductor can be dangerous because consumer protective metalwork may rise in potential.

---

### ii. TT

In a TT system:

- the source has its own earth connection;
- the consumer has a local earth electrode;
- exposed-conductive-parts are connected to that electrode.

The earth-fault path includes the soil/electrode system.

Because this path can have relatively high impedance, fault current may be too low to operate an ordinary overcurrent device quickly.

Therefore RCD fault protection is commonly very important.

---

## (e) Earth Electrode — 2 marks

Formal definition:

> **Earth electrode:** Conductive part, which may be embedded in the soil or in a specific conductive medium, e.g. concrete or coke, in electrical contact with the Earth.

### Practical meaning

The electrode forms an intentional electrical connection between the installation earthing system and the general mass of Earth.

---

## (f) Test Purposes — 4 marks

### i. Earth-electrode resistance test — 2 marks
